docs.title: amlint
docs.text:
A linter for Prometheus Alertmanager configs that finds the bugs nothing else complains about.

amtool check-config tells you whether your config is valid. amlint tells you whether it does what you meant. Does every alert reach someone? Can every route actually match? Does an inhibit rule mute far more than you think? Configs with these bugs load fine and Alertmanager runs without a warning, while alerts quietly go to the wrong place, or nowhere.

Try it in your browser Install

The playground runs amlint inside the page, so your config never leaves your machine.

docs.title: In 30 seconds
docs.text:
pip install amlint
amlint check alertmanager.yml

  ✖  ERROR  [undefined-receiver]  ·  alertmanager.yml:7:7  ·  route.routes[1]
     Route references receiver 'pager' which is not defined in receivers.
     Alertmanager refuses to load this config.

  ⚠  WARN   [unreachable-route]  ·  alertmanager.yml:6:7  ·  route.routes[0]
     Catch-all route (no matchers) with continue:false will intercept all alerts
     — 1 subsequent sibling(s) are unreachable.

  ✖ 1 error  ·  ⚠ 1 warning

Each finding names the check, the exact spot in your file and what will go wrong. The exit code is 1 on any error, so CI fails. Add --strict to fail on warnings too. To see how to fix a finding, run amlint explain <check>, for example amlint explain unreachable-route.

docs.title: What you can do with it
docs.text: I want to… Run Read more Find problems in a config amlint check alertmanager.yml Usage See where an alert would go amlint route alertmanager.yml team=db severity=critical Usage Check whether an alert gets muted amlint route … --firing alertname=NodeDown Usage Write unit tests for routing amlint test alertmanager.yml tests.yml Usage See what a change does to routing amlint diff old.yml new.yml Usage Catch routes for alerts that don't exist amlint check … --rules 'rules/*.yml' Prometheus rules Lint a Secret, Helm values or Mimir config amlint check alertmanager-secret.yaml Kubernetes & Mimir Get findings and a routing diff on every PR the GitHub Action GitHub Action See findings in your editor as you type amlint lsp, started by the editor Editors

docs.title: What it catches
docs.text:
There are 38 checks. 18 of them find configs that amtool accepts but that don't behave the way you expect:

  • Alerts that reach nobody. A route points at a receiver with no integration, or a catch-all route sits above more specific ones.
  • Routes that can never match. An earlier sibling route catches every alert first.
  • Inhibit rules that mute too much. No equal labels, or rules that mute each other.
  • Timings that contradict themselves. For example, group_wait longer than group_interval.
  • Matchers Alertmanager reads differently than you do. For example, code=~[0-9]{3} without quotes loses its closing brace.
  • Routes for alerts that don't exist. With --rules, a typo in an alertname stops being silent.

The other 20 repeat what amtool already rejects, so one tool gives you one report. See all checks.

docs.title: Why not just amtool?
docs.text:
Keep it. amtool is the reference for "is this config valid?", and amlint agrees with it there. amlint adds what comes after that question:

amtool amlint Rejects invalid configs ✅ ✅ Finds valid configs that misroute or over-mute alerts — ✅ Where does one alert go? ✅ ✅ A file of routing tests in CI, with route coverage — ✅ Is this alert muted while that one fires? — ✅ What does this change do to routing? — ✅ Kubernetes, Helm, Mimir and AlertmanagerConfig input — ✅ PR annotations, SARIF, JSON, Markdown output — ✅

The routing and inhibition simulation is checked in CI against real Alertmanager releases, so amlint route and amlint test give the same answers Alertmanager would.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This page gets you from a fresh clone to a pull request: set up, run the tests CI runs, and add a check. The last two sections cover the tests against the real Alertmanager and the browser playground, which you only need when you work on those parts.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/danikdanik2013/amlint
cd amlint
pip install -e ".[dev]"

You need Python 3.9 or later. This installs amlint in editable mode, so amlint runs your working copy, plus pytest, ruff and Hypothesis.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
CI runs these on Python 3.9 to 3.15:

ruff check amlint/
pytest test_linter.py test_formats.py test_lsp.py -v
  • test_linter.py covers the checks and the CLI.
  • test_formats.py covers the input formats on the Kubernetes & Mimir page.
  • Add --cov=amlint for coverage.

docs.title: Add a check
docs.text:
Every check is a function in amlint/linter.py. It takes the parsed config as a dict and returns a list of findings.

1. Write the function.

def check_your_rule(cfg: dict) -> List[Finding]:
    out: List[Finding] = []
    route = _root_route(cfg)
    if not route:
        return out
    for node, path in _walk_routes(route):
        if something_is_wrong(node):
            out.append(Finding(
                WARN,              # ERROR, WARN or INFO
                "your-rule-code",  # unique kebab-case code
                "What's wrong, and what happens to alerts because of it.",
                path,              # where in the config, e.g. route.routes[0]
            ))
    return out

_walk_routes yields every route with its path. The CLI turns the path into file:line:col, in every input format.

2. Register it in ALL_CHECKS in the same file:

ALL_CHECKS = [
    ...
    check_your_rule,
]

3. Explain it. Add an entry for your-rule-code to EXPLAINS in amlint/explains.py, with level, summary, why, bad and good. amlint list and amlint explain read it, and --ignore warns about codes that aren't there. Also add the code to _DOCS_PAGES in the same file, under the docs page you document it on (step 5): editors link each finding to that section.

If Alertmanager refuses to load a config that your check flags, also add the code to ALSO_CAUGHT_BY_AMTOOL in the same file. The differential tests then check that amtool check-config agrees.

4. Add a test to test_linter.py:

def test_your_rule():
    cfg = {
        "route": {"receiver": "a"},
        "receivers": [{"name": "a"}],
        # the smallest config that triggers the rule
    }
    assert "your-rule-code" in codes(cfg)

5. Document it. Add a ## your-rule-code section to the right page under docs/checks/, and a row to the table in docs/checks/index.md. The playground links each finding to its section by that heading.

docs.title: Pick a severity
docs.text: Level Use when ERROR Alertmanager refuses to load the config, or alerts will be lost WARN Almost certainly not what the author meant INFO Suspicious and worth a look, but may be on purpose

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text:
• One check or one fix per pull request is easiest to review.
  • Include a test that fails without your change and passes with it.
  • ruff check amlint/ and pytest test_linter.py test_formats.py test_lsp.py pass.
  • For a new check, add its docs (step 5 above).
  • Add a line to CHANGELOG.md under ## [Unreleased].
  • If you changed the docs, mkdocs build --strict passes (pip install mkdocs-material).

docs.title: Differential tests against Alertmanager
docs.text:
amlint simulates Alertmanager's routing, inhibition and config errors in Python. These tests compare it with the real Alertmanager on generated configs. The fidelity page explains what that guarantees users. Run them with one command:

scripts/differential.sh

The script downloads an Alertmanager release (0.34.1 by default) into .cache/alertmanager/ and checks the tarball's sha256 against the release's sha256sums.txt. Then it runs tests/differential/ with that release's amtool and alertmanager first on PATH. Extra arguments go to pytest.

Test Compares test_routing.py amlint's receivers with amtool config routes test, on generated configs and label sets test_validation.py amtool check-config rejects a config exactly when amlint reports an error whose code is in ALSO_CAUGHT_BY_AMTOOL test_inhibition.py alerts POSTed to a running alertmanager: each one's status.inhibitedBy and receivers with amlint's simulation

Settings, as environment variables:

Variable Default What it sets AM_VERSION 0.34.1 the Alertmanager release AM_SHA256 none the tarball's sha256, checked as well (CI pins it) AMLINT_DIFF_SEED 0 the Hypothesis seed: the same seed generates the same cases AMLINT_DIFF_EXAMPLES 300 generated configs per routing and validation test AMLINT_DIFF_INHIBIT_EXAMPLES 40 inhibition scenarios, each on its own alertmanager 
AM_VERSION=0.32.2 scripts/differential.sh                                  # another release
AMLINT_DIFF_SEED=7 AMLINT_DIFF_EXAMPLES=2000 scripts/differential.sh -x   # explore more
  • The pytest header prints the seed and the number of examples, so you can replay a CI run with the same values.
  • On a mismatch, the test reduces the case to a minimal config and label set. It prints both results and the amtool command that reproduces it.
  • Plain pytest skips these tests when amtool isn't on PATH.

In CI, .github/workflows/differential.yml runs them against the last two minor Alertmanager releases and the newest, on pull requests and pushes to main that touch amlint/routing.py, linter.py, goyaml.py, formats.py, explains.py or the differential tests. It also runs weekly with a fresh seed and more examples, and you can start it by hand with a seed of your choice. When the weekly run warns that a newer Alertmanager is out, add it to the workflow's matrix with its sha256, and update the versions on the fidelity page and in the README.

When a test fails, the mismatch is one of two things:

  • a bug in amlint: fix it, and add a regression test to test_linter.py
  • a deliberate difference or an Alertmanager bug: document it under Known differences, and teach the test to recognize it, narrowly

docs.title: The playground
docs.text:
The playground runs amlint in the browser with Pyodide (Python compiled to WebAssembly).

File What it does docs/playground/app.js the UI docs/playground/worker.js loads Pyodide and amlint in a Web Worker, off the main thread docs/playground/amlint_playground.py calls amlint.cli.main([... "--format", "json"]) for check, route and diff, and builds the route tree overrides/playground.html the page template playground/build.py builds the amlint wheel, the CodeMirror editor bundle and the examples into docs/playground/dist/ (not committed)

New checks show up in the playground without any change there. A change to the JSON output of check, route or diff may need one.

To work on the page locally (needs npm):

pip install mkdocs-material
python playground/build.py   # again after changing amlint/ or playground/
mkdocs serve                 # http://127.0.0.1:8000/amlint/playground/

python playground/build.py --no-editor skips rebuilding the editor bundle, if you already have one.

The docs workflow runs a headless smoke test of the built site on pull requests. To run it yourself:

mkdocs build --strict
python -m http.server 8000 --directory site &
cd playground && npx playwright install chromium && node smoke-test.mjs http://127.0.0.1:8000/playground/

The examples in the playground's menu are listed in EXAMPLES in playground/build.py. Their files are in playground/examples/ and testdata/.

docs.title: Editors
docs.text:
See amlint's findings in your editor as you type, and hover a route to see where its alerts go. amlint lsp is a language server, so it works with VS Code, Neovim, Helix and any other editor that speaks the Language Server Protocol.

You need amlint 0.6.0 or newer:

pip install -U amlint
amlint lsp --help    # check that the command is there

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Findings as you type, on the same lines amlint check reports. amlint lints the editor buffer, so you don't have to save first. Each check code links to its section in these docs.
  • Hover on a route: its matchers and the matchers on the way to it, its receiver, group_by and timings, and where each value comes from: set on this route, inherited from a parent, or Alertmanager's default. It also shows an example alert that ends on the route and the receivers it goes to, from the same simulation as amlint route.
  • Quick fixes for a finding you accept: add # amlint: disable=<code> to its line, or # amlint: disable-file=<code> to the top of the file. See inline suppressions.

A hover over a route looks like this:

Route route.routes[0].routes[0] · amlint

Matchers: severity="critical"

setting          value       from
receiver         db-oncall   set here
group_by         alertname   inherited from route
group_wait       10s         inherited from route.routes[0]
group_interval   5m          Alertmanager default
repeat_interval  4h          Alertmanager default

Alerts that reach it match every route on the way, unless an earlier sibling
route without continue: true takes them first:
- route.routes[0]: team="db"
- route.routes[0].routes[0]: severity="critical"

For example, an alert with team=db, severity=critical ends here and goes to db-oncall.

docs.title: Which files get findings
docs.text:
Every YAML file that holds an Alertmanager config, in any format amlint check reads:

  • a document with route: or receivers: at the top
  • a Kubernetes Secret or ConfigMap with an alertmanager.yaml key
  • kube-prometheus-stack Helm values (alertmanager:), or a Mimir or Cortex config (alertmanager_config:)
  • prometheus-operator AlertmanagerConfig resources

Other YAML files, such as Kubernetes manifests or Prometheus rule files, get nothing. A config that doesn't parse gets one error at the broken line.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Install the amlint extension from the Marketplace: search for "amlint" in the Extensions view, or run:

code --install-extension dpyly.amlint

Then open an alertmanager.yml. The extension runs the amlint you installed, so new checks come with pip install -U amlint, not with an extension update. Settings:

Setting Default What it does amlint.enable true Turn amlint off without uninstalling the extension. amlint.path amlint The amlint executable. ~ and ${workspaceFolder} are expanded, for example ${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/amlint. amlint.trace.server off messages or verbose logs the traffic to the amlint output channel.

amlint: Restart Server in the command palette restarts it, for example after you upgrade amlint. If VS Code says it can't start amlint lsp, run which amlint in a terminal and put that path in amlint.path.

docs.title: Neovim
docs.text:
Neovim 0.11 or newer. In your config:

vim.lsp.config("amlint", {
  cmd = { "amlint", "lsp" },
  filetypes = { "yaml" },
  root_markers = { ".amlint.yml", ".amlint.yaml", ".git" },
})
vim.lsp.enable("amlint")

It runs next to yaml-language-server if you use that too. K shows the hover; quick fixes are in vim.lsp.buf.code_action().

docs.title: Helix
docs.text:
In ~/.config/helix/languages.toml:

[language-server.amlint]
command = "amlint"
args = ["lsp"]

[[language]]
name = "yaml"
language-servers = ["amlint", "yaml-language-server"]

Helix asks the first server in the list for hovers, so put amlint first to get its route hovers.

docs.title: Other editors
docs.text: Configure your LSP client to run amlint lsp over stdio for YAML files. The server needs no initialization options.

docs.title: Configure the checks
docs.text: The editor reads the same project config as the CLI: ignore and severity from .amlint.yml, .amlint.yaml or pyproject.toml in the workspace folder. A file outside any workspace folder uses the config next to it. Edits to the project config apply at the next change to the file; VS Code re-lints open files right away.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The Prometheus rules checks (check --rules) don't run in the editor.
  • template-file-missing looks for template files next to the file on disk, so a new file that was never saved skips it.

docs.title: Verified against Alertmanager
docs.text:
amlint simulates Alertmanager in Python instead of running it. This page shows how CI checks that the simulation matches the real Alertmanager, and lists the few places where it doesn't.

The promise

On generated configs and alerts, amlint gives the same receivers, the same inhibitions and the same rejected configs as Alertmanager 0.32.2, 0.33.1 and 0.34.1.

Each pull request that changes the simulation is checked on 300 routing configs (with several alerts each), 300 configs for config errors and 40 inhibition scenarios, against each of the three versions. A weekly run tries 1,500 + 1,500 + 150 new ones.

What this means for you:

  • amlint route, amlint test and the routing part of amlint diff pick the receivers your Alertmanager would pick, in the same order.
  • amlint route --firing and firing: in tests mute an alert exactly when Alertmanager would.
  • When amlint check reports an error that it marks as also caught by amtool (amlint list shows a ✓), Alertmanager refuses to load the config, and the other way round.
  • Where amlint can't reproduce Alertmanager exactly, such as Unicode classes in regexes (\pL), route and test exit 2 and tell you to use amtool config routes test. They never guess.
  • The exceptions are listed under Known differences.

docs.title: What is compared
docs.text:
amlint Alertmanager Routing the receivers amlint's router returns, in order amtool config routes test --config.file=… label=value … Config errors an error-level finding whose code amlint list marks ✓ (also caught by amtool) amtool check-config rejects the config Inhibition whether amlint's inhibitor mutes each alert status.inhibitedBy from GET /api/v2/alerts on a running alertmanager, after POST /api/v2/alerts

The inhibition test also compares each alert's receivers from the API, which is a second, independent routing check against the server itself.

How the job runs (.github/workflows/differential.yml):

  • Versions: the last two minor releases and the newest, 0.32.2, 0.33.1 and 0.34.1. It downloads the official release tarballs and checks their sha256 against values pinned in the workflow. A weekly job warns when a newer Alertmanager release is out.
  • When: on pull requests and pushes to main that change the simulation, the checks, how configs are read, or the tests, and weekly.
  • Cases: Hypothesis, a property-based testing library, generates the configs and alerts from a seed. Pull requests and pushes use seed 0, so every run tests the same cases. The weekly run uses a fresh seed to find new ones.

docs.title: What the generated configs cover
docs.text:
• route trees up to four levels deep, with continue: true / false fan-out and inherited receivers
  • =, !=, =~ and !~ matchers in every spelling Alertmanager accepts: matchers: entries with one or several matchers, with or without {}, quoted, loosely escaped ("a\.b") or bare values, spaces around the operator, quoted label names ("service.name"="api"), and match: / match_re: maps
  • regexes from a pool of real-world patterns and built from parts: alternations, groups, classes, quantifiers, ^ $ \A \z \b \B, (?i), (?s), (?m)
  • label values that stress quoting and matching: quotes, backslashes, commas, braces, newlines, non-ASCII letters (é, the Kelvin sign), and plain YAML scalars that YAML 1.1 would type (NO, 1.10, 0x1F)
  • label sets with labels missing, empty, or set to values the matchers look for
  • configs with up to two of the mistakes amtool check-config rejects, including integration fields covered (or not) by a _file variant or a global: default, matchers: entries that neither matcher parser reads, and match: / match_re: keys that aren't classic label names (k8s.ns, 1a, a null key)
  • inhibit rules with equal:, rules matching both sides, and alerts that match several rules

When amlint and Alertmanager disagree, the test reduces the case to a minimal config and label set that still disagree. It prints both results and the amtool command that reproduces it. To run the tests yourself, see Contributing.

docs.title: Known differences
docs.text:
Each of these is deliberate, depends on how Alertmanager was built, or is an Alertmanager bug. The tests recognize each one narrowly and count it in their statistics, so none is skipped silently.

  • Inhibition before Alertmanager 0.34.1. Older releases keep one source alert per inhibit rule and equal: value. If that alert matches both sides of the rule, they miss the inhibition, even when another firing alert would inhibit. So the result depends on the order the alerts arrived. 0.34.1 fixed this (#5449, #5542, #5559), and amlint follows 0.34.1. If you run 0.32 or 0.33, Alertmanager may not mute an alert that amlint says is muted, but only when another firing alert matches both sides of the rule.
  • Regexes amlint declines. Python can't evaluate Unicode classes (\pL, \p{Greek}) or negated POSIX classes ([[:^alpha:]]) the way Go does. For these, amlint route and amlint test exit 2 and point you to amtool config routes test. amlint check still accepts them as valid regexes.
  • Unknown Unicode class names. amlint check doesn't report a \p{...} class Go doesn't know, such as \p{Foo}, but Alertmanager rejects it ("invalid character class range"). Which names are valid depends on the Go version Alertmanager was built with: Go 1.25 added aliases such as \p{Letter} and made names case-insensitive. So \p{greek} works in Alertmanager 0.32 to 0.34 (built with Go 1.26), but not in builds with older Go.
  • Configs Alertmanager won't load. amlint route and amlint test still simulate a config with errors that amlint check reports, such as an undefined receiver or a root route without a receiver. amlint diff relies on this to compare a new file against an empty config. The config-error test covers these errors through amlint check.

docs.title: Alertmanager behavior amlint matches
docs.text:
The differential tests found these surprising Alertmanager behaviors. amlint now behaves the same way, and amlint check reports the cases that are probably not what you meant.

  • YAML scalars. Alertmanager reads match: {country: NO} as the string NO, although YAML 1.1 says false. 1.10, 0x1F, yes and the like keep their text too, in a plain config and in one held in a Secret or a Mimir config. Helm values are different: Helm reads values.yaml as YAML 1.1 before it renders the config, so there NO really is false, and amlint reads it that way.
  • Bare regexes with braces. Alertmanager strips one trailing } from a matchers: entry even when the entry doesn't start with {. So a bare code=~[0-9]{3} is the regex [0-9]{3, which matches 1{3 and not 123. Quote the value (code=~"[0-9]{3}") to get what you meant. amlint check warns about it (stripped-brace).
  • Which matcher parser reads an entry. Alertmanager has two matcher parsers: the classic one and a newer UTF-8 one. The classic parser reads an entry whenever it can, even where the UTF-8 one would read it differently. Only when it fails, for example on a quoted label name, does the UTF-8 parser read the whole entry, with Go string escapes: there \t is a tab and \. is an error. Bare values are unescaped like quoted ones (a=x\\y is x\y). amlint check reports an entry neither parser reads as bad-matcher.
  • Regex details. \b and \B look at ASCII word characters only and ignore (?i), and \B matches an empty value. $ outside (?m) doesn't match before a final newline. A quantifier after an anchor (^*, \b+) is valid in Go; [\b] is not.
  • Config errors. group_by: ['...', alertname] is an error, since Alertmanager refuses it. An empty api_url: "" in slack_configs is an error, even with global.slack_api_url set. match: keys that aren't classic label names (k8s.ns) are rejected (bad-match-label); use a quoted name in matchers: for those.

docs.title: Not covered yet
docs.text:
• Alerts use label names from a small pool.
  • group_by, timings and time intervals aren't compared, because amtool doesn't print them. The inhibition test reads only receivers and inhibitions from the API.
  • Only matchers: entries, match: maps, receivers and inhibit rules are generated. Integration settings beyond the fields amlint checks, templates, and YAML features such as anchors and merge keys are not.

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text: Run amlint on every push and pull request with one workflow step. Findings show up as annotations on the pull request diff, the job fails on errors, and the action can post a comment that shows which alerts a change routes differently.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/alertmanager.yml
name: Lint Alertmanager config

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: danikdanik2013/amlint@v0.6.1
        with:
          config-path: alertmanager.yml

Each finding becomes an annotation on the line it points at. The job fails on ERROR findings; add strict: true to fail on WARN findings too.

config-path can be a plain alertmanager.yml or any file from Kubernetes & Mimir: a Secret, Helm values, a Mimir config or AlertmanagerConfig resources. amlint detects the format from the content.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Default What it does config-path required The file to lint (one file) strict false Fail on WARN as well as ERROR (--strict) ignore "" Comma-separated check codes to skip (--ignore) only "" Comma-separated check codes to run, and no others (--only) format github github: findings become annotations. text: the console report in the job log sarif false Also upload findings to GitHub code scanning as SARIF (below) diff-base "" Git ref to compare config-path against; posts the routing diff as a PR comment (below) github-token github.token Token used to post the routing diff comment version "" (latest) amlint version to install from PyPI, e.g. 0.6.1 (below)

docs.title: Post the routing diff on pull requests
docs.text:
Set diff-base to the pull request's base commit. The action then compares your config with its version at that commit, using amlint diff --format markdown, and posts the result as one PR comment. Each push updates the same comment. When routes changed, the comment includes a diagram of them.

# .github/workflows/alertmanager.yml
name: Lint Alertmanager config

on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # to create and update the comment

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # the base commit has to be in the checkout
      - uses: danikdanik2013/amlint@v0.6.1
        with:
          config-path: alertmanager.yml
          diff-base: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}

The comment has a summary line, then the label sets (combinations of alert labels) whose receivers changed, changed group_by and timings, and new and fixed findings with their file:line:col. Sections with nothing in them are left out. For example:

(+1 similar) means one more label set has exactly the same change.

How it behaves:

  • Pull requests only. It runs on pull_request and pull_request_target events. On other events, such as a push, the step is skipped.
  • One comment. The comment starts with a hidden <!-- amlint-routing-diff --> marker, which is how the action finds it again. It posts with curl and the GitHub REST API, with no third-party actions.
  • New config. If the file doesn't exist at the base commit, it is new in the PR. The diff runs against an empty config, so every finding is new and every receiver was (none) before.
  • No change. If the file is the same as at the base and there is no comment yet, nothing is posted. An existing comment is still updated, so it doesn't go stale after a revert.
  • Job summary. The report is also written to the job summary. Look there on pull requests from forks: their GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only, so the comment can't be posted, and the step logs a warning instead of failing.
  • Never fails on findings. The routing diff is informational. If amlint diff can't read a config, the step logs a warning and posts nothing.

  • Needs the base commit. If the base commit isn't in the checkout, the step fails and says how to fix it. fetch-depth: 0 is the simplest fix. Fetching only the base commit works too:

          - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: git fetch --no-tags --depth=1 origin ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}

  • ignore and only apply to the findings in the comment too.

  • A report longer than GitHub allows in a comment is cut at 65,000 characters. Run amlint diff locally for the rest.

docs.title: amlint diff
docs.text: 2 routing changes · no new findings · 0 fixed · 0 unchanged · 6 label sets checked

docs.title: Receivers
docs.text: labels before after team=db, severity=critical pagerduty-db slack-db

docs.title: Grouping and timings
docs.text:
labels receiver setting before after team=infra (+1 similar) infra-slack group_wait 30s 10s

Compared with alertmanager.yml at 3f2c1a9d8e7b. Updated on every push.

docs.title: Upload to code scanning
docs.text:
To also see findings in the repository's Security tab, turn on sarif. The repository needs GitHub code scanning (free for public repositories).

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: danikdanik2013/amlint@v0.6.1
        with:
          config-path: alertmanager.yml
          sarif: true
  • The SARIF upload runs even when the check finds problems, so code scanning shows them on the same run that fails.
  • The job still fails on ERROR findings. To get code scanning annotations only, without the github format's annotations, also set format: text.
  • ignore and only apply to the SARIF upload too.

docs.title: Pin the amlint version
docs.text:
By default the action installs the latest amlint from PyPI, so a new release with new checks can start failing your build. To choose when you upgrade, set version:

      - uses: danikdanik2013/amlint@v0.6.1
        with:
          config-path: alertmanager.yml
          version: '0.6.1'

Don't pin below 0.4.1: the default format: github needs 0.4.0, and diff-base needs 0.4.1. The formats on the Kubernetes & Mimir page need 0.5.0 or later, and the Changed routes diagram in the PR comment needs 0.6.0.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• config-path takes one file. To lint several, add a step per file.

  • There are no inputs for --input-format, --matcher-strategy or --rules. If you need them, install amlint and run it yourself:

          - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: pip install amlint
      - run: amlint check values.yaml --input-format helm --format github

docs.title: Install
docs.text: Pick whichever fits how you work. Or don't install anything: the playground runs amlint in your browser.

docs.title: pip
docs.text:
pip install amlint

You need Python 3.9 or newer. amlint pulls in two small dependencies, PyYAML and Rich.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
No Python needed. Mount the folder with your config and pass its path inside the container:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/cfg ghcr.io/danikdanik2013/amlint check /cfg/alertmanager.yml

Releases are tagged by version (0.6.1) and minor version (0.6); latest follows the main branch.

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text:
brew tap danikdanik2013/amlint https://github.com/danikdanik2013/amlint
brew install amlint

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text: Nothing to install. Add the action to a workflow; see GitHub Action.

docs.title: pre-commit
docs.text:
Check the config on every commit. Add this to .pre-commit-config.yaml:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/danikdanik2013/amlint
    rev: v0.6.1
    hooks:
      - id: amlint

The hook runs on files whose names end in alertmanager.yml or alertmanager.yaml.

docs.title: Editors
docs.text:
To see findings as you type, install amlint as above, then:

  • VS Code: install the amlint extension (code --install-extension dpyly.amlint).
  • Neovim, Helix and others: see Editors.

docs.title: AI coding assistants
docs.text:
Claude Code: add the plugin. It teaches Claude to run amlint when you ask it to check an Alertmanager config, explain a finding, trace where an alert goes or write routing tests:

/plugin marketplace add danikdanik2013/amlint
/plugin install amlint@amlint

You still need amlint itself installed (see above). The plugin only tells Claude how to use it.

Other assistants: llms.txt is a short summary of amlint for AI tools, and llms-full.txt has every page of these docs in one file.

docs.title: Shell completions
docs.text:
Tab completion for commands and flags in bash and zsh:

pip install "amlint[completions]"

# bash
echo 'eval "$(register-python-argcomplete amlint)"' >> ~/.bashrc

# zsh
echo 'eval "$(register-python-argcomplete amlint)"' >> ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
amlint --version
amlint init > /tmp/alertmanager.yml && amlint check /tmp/alertmanager.yml

amlint init prints a minimal valid config, so the second command should report no errors.

docs.title: Kubernetes & Mimir
docs.text: Lint the file you actually deploy: a Kubernetes Secret, kube-prometheus-stack Helm values, a Mimir or Cortex tenant config, or prometheus-operator AlertmanagerConfig resources. You don't need to extract alertmanager.yml first, and findings point at the line in the file you gave amlint.

docs.title: Point amlint at the file you deploy
docs.text:
amlint check alertmanager-secret.yaml                    # Secret or ConfigMap
amlint check values.yaml                                 # kube-prometheus-stack values
amlint check tenant-config.yaml                          # Mimir / Cortex
amlint route alertmanagerconfigs.yaml namespace=team-a severity=critical
kubectl kustomize deploy/monitoring | amlint check -     # a whole stream on stdin

check, diff, tree, route and test all read these formats. amlint detects the format from the content:

If the file has… amlint reads it as It lints Findings point at a kind: AlertmanagerConfig anywhere alertmanagerconfig the resources, merged into the base config the way the operator merges them (details) the line in the resource a Secret or ConfigMap with an alertmanager.yaml, alertmanager.yml or alertmanager.yaml.gz key secret that key; the other keys are template files in a literal block (key: |): the exact line. Base64 or a quoted string: the key a top-level alertmanager_config: string mimir that string, plus template_files in a literal block: the exact line. Otherwise: the key a top-level alertmanager: map, and no top-level route: or receivers: helm alertmanager.config merged over the chart's defaults, plus alertmanager.templateFiles the line in the values file none of the above alertmanager the file as a plain config the line in the file
  • A file can be a stream of YAML documents (---) or a kind: List, as kubectl get -o yaml prints it. amlint skips other objects in it (Deployments, Services, PrometheusRules, and Secrets or ConfigMaps without a config key).
  • amlint lints one config per file. A file with two configs (two config Secrets, say) exits 2: split it, or, if the two are in different formats, pick one with --input-format. A file with no config at all also exits 2.
  • note: lines on stderr say how amlint read the file, for example which parts of a Helm config come from the chart. They don't change the exit code.

To skip detection, pass --input-format with auto (the default), alertmanager, secret, helm, mimir or alertmanagerconfig. --input-format alertmanager reads the file as one plain document, even if it looks like something else.

docs.title: Secrets and ConfigMaps
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: alertmanager-main
  namespace: monitoring
stringData:
  alertmanager.yaml: |-
    route:
      receiver: default
      ...
  notify.tmpl: |-
    {{ define "notify.description" }}...{{ end }}
  • Use a literal block (alertmanager.yaml: |, YAML's multi-line string that keeps line breaks). Then every finding points at its line and column inside the block, and # amlint: disable=... comments inside the block work as in a plain file. With base64 data or a quoted string, lines can't be mapped one to one, so findings point at the alertmanager.yaml: key.
  • stringData wins over data for the same key, as the API server merges them. data values are base64.
  • alertmanager.yaml.gz is the gzipped, base64 config in the Secret the operator generates (alertmanager-<name>-generated).
  • Template files. The Secret's other keys are template files. The operator mounts them in /etc/alertmanager/config/, so amlint checks templates: entries in that directory against the keys instead of against files on disk:
    • a file name that isn't a key is an error
    • a glob that matches no key is a warning, but only if the Secret has template files at all (*.tmpl with no template files just loads nothing)
    • relative paths and other directories aren't checked. The operator runs Alertmanager on a copy of the config in config_out/, so they don't resolve next to the Secret.
  • A ConfigMap is read the same way, from data or base64 binaryData. Its template files aren't checked, because where it is mounted depends on how you deploy it.

docs.title: kube-prometheus-stack Helm values
docs.text:
alertmanager:
  config:
    route:
      receiver: slack
    receivers:
      - name: slack
        slack_configs:
          - api_url: https://hooks.slack.com/services/T/B/X

Helm merges your values over the chart's own values.yaml, so Alertmanager gets more than your file says. amlint merges alertmanager.config over the default config of kube-prometheus-stack 92.10.1 the same way: maps key by key, lists replaced whole, and null deletes a key.

That catches a common mistake. The values above replace receivers, so the chart's null receiver is gone, but the chart's Watchdog route to null is still there:

$ amlint check values.yaml
note: values.yaml:2: alertmanager.config is merged over the kube-prometheus-stack 92.10.1 defaults, as Helm merges values: global, inhibit_rules, templates, route.routes come from the chart

  ✖  ERROR  [undefined-receiver]  ·  values.yaml:3:5  ·  route.routes[0]
     Route references receiver 'null' which is not defined in receivers. Alertmanager refuses to load this config.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ✖ 1 error

A finding in a part that only the chart's defaults have points at the nearest part your file does have: here, the route: that the default routes are merged into.

  • alertmanager.templateFiles end up in the config Secret, so templates: entries in /etc/alertmanager/config/ are checked against them, as for a Secret.
  • alertmanager.stringConfig is used only with alertmanager.tplConfig: true, as in the chart's Secret template. Without it the chart renders alertmanager.config, and amlint notes that the string is ignored. A string alertmanager.config is read as a config.
  • alertmanager.alertmanagerSpec.alertmanagerConfigMatcherStrategy.type sets the matcher strategy for AlertmanagerConfig resources in the same stream.

  • Values from --set or other values files aren't in the file. Lint the values Helm actually uses, or the rendered chart, which holds the config Secret:

    helm get values <release> --all -o yaml | amlint check -
helm template monitoring ./chart | amlint check -

docs.title: Mimir and Cortex
docs.text:
This is the format mimirtool alertmanager get prints and POST /api/v1/alerts takes:

template_files:
  default_template: |
    {{ define "email.subject" }}...{{ end }}
alertmanager_config: |
  route:
    receiver: team-email
  ...

amlint doesn't check templates: against template_files: Mimir loads every template file of the tenant, whatever templates: lists, and refuses entries that contain a path.

docs.title: prometheus-operator AlertmanagerConfig
docs.text:
AlertmanagerConfig resources (monitoring.coreos.com/v1alpha1 and v1beta1) let each team define its own routes and receivers in its own namespace. The operator converts them and merges them into one Alertmanager config. amlint does the same, the way prometheus-operator v0.94.1 does it, so findings, tree, route and test show the config Alertmanager will actually run.

$ amlint tree alertmanagerconfigs.yaml

   (root)  →  default
├──    {namespace="team-a"}  →  team-a/payments/slack  [continue]
│   └──    {severity="critical"}  →  team-a/payments/pager
├──    {service=~"search-.*", namespace="team-b"}  →  team-b/search/webhook  [continue]
└──    {alertname = "Watchdog"}  →  null

  1 more issue outside routing (receivers, global, timing) — run 'amlint check alertmanagerconfigs.yaml' for full details.
alertmanagerconfigs.yaml: a config Secret and two teams' resources 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: alertmanager-main
  namespace: monitoring
stringData:
  alertmanager.yaml: |
    global:
      resolve_timeout: 5m
    route:
      receiver: default
      routes:
        - matchers: ['alertname = "Watchdog"']
          receiver: "null"
    receivers:
      - name: default
        webhook_configs:
          - url: http://example.com/default
      - name: "null"
---
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: AlertmanagerConfig
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  route:
    receiver: slack
    routes:
      - matchers:
          - name: severity
            value: critical
        receiver: pager
  receivers:
    - name: slack
      slackConfigs:
        - apiURL:
            name: slack-webhook
            key: url
          channel: '#payments'
    - name: pager
      pagerdutyConfigs:
        - routingKey:
            name: pagerduty
            key: routing-key
---
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1beta1
kind: AlertmanagerConfig
metadata:
  name: search
  namespace: team-b
spec:
  route:
    receiver: webhook
    matchers:
      - name: service
        value: search-.*
        matchType: "=~"
  receivers:
    - name: webhook
      webhookConfigs:
        - url: http://search.example.com/hook

What the merge does:

  • Names. Receiver and time interval names become <namespace>/<name>/<receiver>, so receiver: pager in team-a/payments is team-a/payments/pager. Findings, tree, route and test all use these names.
  • Namespace matcher. Each resource's route gets namespace="<namespace>" added to its matchers, and so do both sides of each of its inhibit rules (unless a side already has it). So a resource only sees alerts from its own namespace. The matcher strategy can turn this off.
  • Order and continue. The resources' routes go first under the root route, sorted by namespace/name, before the base config's own routes. Each gets continue: true, so alerts also go on to the routes after it.
  • Base config. A Secret, plain config, Helm values or Mimir config in the same stream is the base. Without one, amlint uses the operator's default config (a root route to a null receiver) and drops findings about that default, since there is nothing in your input to fix.
  • Secret references. Fields that reference a Secret (apiURL, routingKey, apiKey, urlSecret, botToken, ...) count as set, because the operator fills in the value. amlint doesn't read the value, so it can't catch a Secret that doesn't exist.
  • Field names. camelCase fields become Alertmanager's (slackConfigs → slack_configs, groupWait → group_wait). A webhook's urlSecret becomes its url, a Discord apiURL its webhook_url. A zero groupInterval or repeatInterval is dropped, as the operator drops it, so the parent's value applies.
  • API versions. v1alpha1 calls the top-level time intervals muteTimeIntervals, v1beta1 calls them timeIntervals. If a resource uses the other version's name, amlint notes that the API server drops it. A v1alpha1 matcher without matchType uses regex: true for =~.
  • No spec.route. A resource without a route only contributes its inhibit rules. The operator drops its receivers and time intervals, and amlint notes it.
  • spec.alertmanagerConfiguration. If an Alertmanager resource in the input names one of the resources there, that resource becomes the whole config, without a namespace matcher, as the operator does it.

Some findings would only describe what the operator adds on purpose, so amlint drops them: inhibit-same-match, inhibit-no-equal and circular-inhibition when only the namespace matcher causes them, and useless-continue on a resource's route. Problems in your own rules are still reported.

docs.title: Matcher strategy
docs.text:
alertmanagerConfigMatcherStrategy decides which resources get the namespace matcher:

Strategy Namespace matcher OnNamespace (default) added to every resource OnNamespaceExceptForAlertmanagerNamespace added, except to resources in the Alertmanager's own namespace None never added

amlint takes the first of these it finds: --matcher-strategy, an Alertmanager resource in the input (spec.alertmanagerConfigMatcherStrategy.type), Helm values in the input (alertmanager.alertmanagerSpec.alertmanagerConfigMatcherStrategy.type). Otherwise it uses OnNamespace.

For OnNamespaceExceptForAlertmanagerNamespace, the Alertmanager's namespace comes from the Alertmanager resource or the config Secret. If neither is in the input, every resource gets the matcher, and amlint notes it.

docs.title: Routing tests
docs.text:
Test cases run against the merged config. So their labels need a namespace, and they use the operator's receiver names:

tests:
  - name: payments critical alerts page
    labels: {namespace: team-a, alertname: PaymentsDown, severity: critical}
    expect: team-a/payments/pager
  - name: another namespace never reaches team-a
    labels: {namespace: team-c, alertname: PaymentsDown, severity: critical}
    expect: default
  - name: team-a's route has continue, so the base routes still see its alerts
    labels: {namespace: team-a, alertname: Watchdog}
    expect: [team-a/payments/slack, "null"]

$ amlint test alertmanagerconfigs.yaml routing-tests.yaml
  ✓  payments critical alerts page
  ✓  another namespace never reaches team-a
  ✓  team-a's route has continue, so the base routes still see its alerts
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  3 passed

docs.title: Lint several files together
docs.text:
The operator merges every selected resource, and amlint merges every resource in one input. To lint resources from several files together, send them as one stream:

kubectl kustomize deploy/monitoring | amlint check -
helm template monitoring ./chart | amlint check -
kubectl get alertmanagerconfigs -A -o yaml | amlint check -
for f in alertmanagerconfigs/*.yaml; do echo ---; cat "$f"; done | amlint check -

With stdin, findings point at lines of the stream. amlint check a.yaml b.yaml instead lints each file on its own, so each resource is merged into the operator's default config.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• alertmanagerConfigSelector and alertmanagerConfigNamespaceSelector aren't modeled: every resource in the input counts as selected.
  • The operator's validation isn't modeled. The operator skips a whole resource it rejects (say, a route to a receiver the resource doesn't define). amlint reports what is wrong instead.
  • Matchers are always written in the matchers: syntax, so configs for Alertmanager before 0.22 aren't modeled.
  • A resource without metadata.namespace is taken to be in default, with a note.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: amlint finds mistakes in an Alertmanager config before they cost you a missed page. It also shows where a given alert ends up, runs routing tests in CI, and shows how a change reroutes alerts.

docs.title: In 60 seconds
docs.text:
amlint check alertmanager.yml                                # find mistakes
amlint route alertmanager.yml team=infra severity=critical   # where does this alert go?
amlint test alertmanager.yml routing-tests.yml               # run your routing tests
amlint diff main.yml alertmanager.yml                        # what does this change break or reroute?
Command Use it to check find mistakes in one or more configs tree print the routing tree with problems marked on it route see where an alert with given labels goes test run routing unit tests from a file diff compare two configs: new and fixed findings, and alerts that now go elsewhere list, explain see every check, or read about one init print a minimal valid config to start from lsp show findings in your editor as you type amlint --version print the installed version

docs.title: Find mistakes in a config
docs.text:
check reviews the whole config: routes (the tree of label conditions, called matchers, that decides where each alert goes), receivers (named notification targets, such as a Slack channel), inhibit rules (rules that mute some alerts while a related alert fires), timings and integration settings.

amlint check alertmanager.yml
amlint check prod.yml staging.yml        # several files
cat alertmanager.yml | amlint check -    # stdin

  ✖  ERROR  [undefined-receiver]  ·  alertmanager.yml:6:7  ·  route.routes[1]
     Route references receiver 'db-pager' which is not defined in receivers. Alertmanager refuses to load this config.

  ℹ  INFO   [global-resolve-timeout-missing]  ·  alertmanager.yml:1:1  ·  global
     global.resolve_timeout is not set, so Alertmanager uses 5m. It only applies to alerts sent without an end time; Prometheus always sets one.

────────────────────────────────────────
  ✖ 1 error  ·  ℹ 1 info

Each finding shows:

  • its level: ERROR, WARN or INFO. By default only ERROR fails the run.
  • the check code. amlint explain <code> tells you why it matters and how to fix it.
  • file:line:col, which most terminals and editors turn into a link.
  • the config path: route.routes[1] is the second child of the top-level route.

Options

Flag What it does --strict Exit 1 on WARN findings too, not only ERROR --exit-zero Always exit 0 when the config could be read, whatever amlint finds. For report-only CI runs --ignore CODE Skip these checks. Comma-separate the codes or repeat the flag --only CODE Report only these checks. Comma-separate the codes or repeat the flag --format FORMAT text (default), json, sarif (Code Scanning) or github (PR annotations) --rules GLOB Also check against your Prometheus alerting rules. Quote the glob; repeat the flag for more (details) --input-format FORMAT What the file is: auto (default, detected), alertmanager, secret, helm, mimir or alertmanagerconfig (details) --matcher-strategy STRATEGY alertmanagerConfigMatcherStrategy for AlertmanagerConfig resources: OnNamespace, OnNamespaceExceptForAlertmanagerNamespace or None. Default: the one on the Alertmanager resource in the input, else OnNamespace

Good to know

  • The line is where that part of the config starts: the - entry of a route, receiver or inhibit rule, or a key such as global:. If the part is missing (no global: block), the finding points at the nearest part that exists. JSON and SARIF carry the same line and column.
  • With several files, text output has one section per file.
  • A misspelled code in --ignore, --only or a config file prints a warning with a "did you mean" suggestion instead of being silently ignored.

docs.title: Kubernetes, Helm and Mimir
docs.text: Besides a plain alertmanager.yml, amlint reads a Kubernetes Secret or ConfigMap holding alertmanager.yaml, kube-prometheus-stack Helm values, a Mimir or Cortex tenant config, and prometheus-operator AlertmanagerConfig resources, which it merges the way the operator does. It detects the format; --input-format overrides that. Findings point at the line in the file you passed. diff, tree, route and test take --input-format and --matcher-strategy too. See Kubernetes & Mimir.

docs.title: Get JSON output
docs.text:
amlint check alertmanager.yml --format json

The output is a list with one object per finding:

{
  "file": "alertmanager.yml",
  "line": 6,
  "column": 7,
  "level": "error",
  "code": "undefined-receiver",
  "message": "Route references receiver 'db-pager' which is not defined in receivers. Alertmanager refuses to load this config.",
  "where": "route.routes[1]"
}

level is error, warn or info. file is - for stdin.

docs.title: Set defaults for a repo
docs.text:
amlint reads settings from .amlint.yml (or .amlint.yaml) in the directory you run it from. If there is none, it reads [tool.amlint] from pyproject.toml in that directory.

.amlint.ymlpyproject.toml 
ignore:
  - empty-receiver
  - unused-receiver
strict: true
severity:
  empty-receiver: info      # downgrade warn → info
  unused-receiver: error    # upgrade info → error

[tool.amlint]
ignore = ["empty-receiver", "unused-receiver"]
strict = true

[tool.amlint.severity]
empty-receiver = "info"
unused-receiver = "error"
Key What it does Used by ignore Checks to skip, added to any --ignore codes check, diff, tree, lsp strict Same as --strict check severity Sets a check's level to error, warn or info check, diff, tree, lsp

Good to know: amlint doesn't look in parent directories or next to the config file. Only the first file found is read, so pyproject.toml is ignored when .amlint.yml exists.

docs.title: Silence one finding in the config
docs.text:
Turn a check off for one spot with a comment. The exception and its reason then live next to the config, not in a global ignore: list:

# amlint: disable-file=global-resolve-timeout-missing

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: catch-all   # amlint: disable=unreachable-route
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: infra

receivers:
  # amlint: disable=empty-receiver, unused-receiver
  # drops alerts on purpose
  - name: blackhole
Comment Where Silences # amlint: disable=code1,code2 at the end of a line those codes for findings on that line # amlint: disable=code1,code2 on a line of its own those codes for findings on the next line of YAML (other comment lines in between are fine) # amlint: disable-file=code1,code2 in the comment block at the top of the file, before any YAML those codes for the whole file

Good to know

  • A finding's line is the one shown in the output.
  • An unknown code gets the same "did you mean" warning as --ignore. A disable-file comment further down the file is ignored, with a warning.
  • Suppressions also apply to diff, tree and the editor, which can add the comment for you.

docs.title: Check routes against your Prometheus rules
docs.text:
On its own, amlint only sees the Alertmanager config. Give it your alerting rules with --rules, and it also checks that routes and inhibit rules match alerts that actually exist:

amlint check alertmanager.yml --rules 'rules/*.yml'
amlint check alertmanager.yml --rules 'rules/**/*.yml' --rules 'manifests/*-prometheusrule.yaml'

  ⚠  WARN   [route-unknown-alertname]  ·  alertmanager.yml:7:7  ·  route.routes[0]
     Route matches alertname 'HighCpuUsage', which no alerting rule in the --rules files produces — did you mean 'HighCPUUsage'? Unless such alerts come from another source, this branch is dead.

--rules adds three checks:

Code Level What it catches route-unknown-alertname warn A route matches an alertname no rule produces (typo, renamed or removed rule), with a "did you mean" inhibit-unknown-alertname warn The same for an inhibit rule's source and target matchers alert-hits-default-receiver info Based on their static labels, alerts match no child route and go to the root receiver (one finding per severity=… etc.)

Good to know

  • --rules reads Prometheus rule files (groups:) and prometheus-operator PrometheusRule manifests (spec.groups:). Recording rules are skipped. ** matches subdirectories.
  • Quote the glob. Unquoted, the shell expands it, and the extra files are either rejected as unknown arguments or linted as Alertmanager configs, depending on where --rules sits. amlint warns when a config looks like a rule file.
  • A glob that matches no files, a directory instead of a glob, or a rule file that doesn't parse exits 2. If the files hold no alerting rules, amlint warns and skips the three checks.
  • amlint only knows alertname and the rule's labels:. Real alerts also get labels from their PromQL series and Prometheus' external_labels, so a templated label value counts as unknown, and a result that depends on an unknown label is skipped rather than guessed. See Prometheus rules checks.

docs.title: See the routing tree
docs.text:
tree prints the route tree with problems marked inline, so you can see how alerts flow without reading the YAML:

amlint tree alertmanager.yml
cat alertmanager.yml | amlint tree -   # stdin

   (root)  →  default
├──    {team="infra"}  →  infra-slack  [continue]
├── ⚠  (catch-all)  →  catch-all  (unreachable-route)
└── ✖  {severity="critical"}  →  pager-team  (undefined-receiver)

  2 routing issues flagged above — run 'amlint check alertmanager.yml' for full details.

  2 more issues outside routing (receivers, global, timing) — run 'amlint check alertmanager.yml' for full details.

Each line is one route:

  • its matchers, or (catch-all) if it has none,
  • → the receiver it sends to, or (inherited) if it doesn't set one,
  • [continue] when the route has continue: true, which tells Alertmanager to keep checking the next sibling routes after this one matches,
  • the level icon and check codes when a routing check (undefined-receiver, unreachable-route, route-match-collision, bad-regex, groupby-ellipsis and similar) fired on that route.

Findings that don't belong to one route (receivers, global settings, timing) are counted below the tree.

Options

Flag What it does --ignore CODE Don't mark these checks on the tree. Comma-separate the codes or repeat the flag --format mermaid Print a Mermaid flowchart instead of the text tree --input-format, --matcher-strategy As for check

Good to know: tree exits 0 even when it marks problems. Use check to fail CI.

docs.title: Draw the tree as a diagram
docs.text:
--format mermaid prints the tree as a Mermaid flowchart. Put it in a ```mermaid block and GitHub, GitLab and MkDocs draw it:

amlint tree broken.yml --format mermaid

flowchart LR
    r["(root)<br/>→ default-team<br/>✖ groupby-ellipsis"]
    r_0["(catch-all)<br/>→ catch-all-team<br/>⚠ unreachable-route"]
    r --> r_0
    r_1["{severity=#34;critical#34;}<br/>→ pager-team<br/>✖ undefined-receiver"]
    r --> r_1
    r_2["{service=~#34;auth([#34;}<br/>→ default-team<br/>✖ bad-regex"]
    r --> r_2
    classDef error fill:#ffebe9,stroke:#cf222e,color:#1f2328
    class r,r_1,r_2 error
    classDef warn fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700,color:#1f2328
    class r_0 warn
  • Each node shows the matchers, the receiver and continue. Routes with an error are red, routes with a warning are yellow, and the check codes are on the node.
  • Text from the config is written as Mermaid entity codes (#34; is a quote), so a receiver name can't break the diagram.
  • A tree with more than 150 routes stops there, with …and N more routes.

docs.title: See where an alert goes
docs.text:
route simulates Alertmanager's routing for one alert. It shows which routes the alert matches, which receivers get it, and the grouping and timings it ends up with: group_by (the labels Alertmanager uses to batch alerts into one notification), group_wait (how long it waits before sending the first notification for a new batch), group_interval and repeat_interval.

amlint route alertmanager.yml team=infra severity=critical alertname=DiskFull

  Labels  team=infra, severity=critical, alertname=DiskFull

  1. route → route.routes[0] → route.routes[0].routes[0]
    receiver          infra-pager          set here
    group_by          alertname, cluster   inherited from route
    group_wait        10s                  inherited from route.routes[0]
    group_interval    5m                   Alertmanager default
    repeat_interval   1h                   set here

  2. route → route.routes[1]
    receiver          pager                set here
    group_by          alertname, cluster   inherited from route
    group_wait        30s                  Alertmanager default
    group_interval    5m                   Alertmanager default
    repeat_interval   4h                   Alertmanager default

────────────────────────────────────────
  Delivered to: infra-pager, pager

Here route.routes[0] has continue: true. So after the alert reaches its critical child, route.routes[1] is checked too, and matches as well. The last column says where each value comes from. mute_time_intervals and active_time_intervals show up when the matched route sets them.

Pass labels as label=value. With no labels, amlint routes an alert that has none. Unlike amtool config routes test, route also shows the effective grouping and timings and where each comes from, and it needs no Go binary.

How amlint matches, following Alertmanager:

  • Routes are checked depth-first, children in order. A route matches when all its matchers match. The first matching child ends the search at its level, unless it has continue: true. If no child matches, the parent itself is the match.
  • receiver, group_by and the timings are inherited from the parent. Alertmanager's defaults are 30s / 5m / 4h. group_by: [] means no grouping, and group_by: ['...'] groups by every label. Time intervals are not inherited: each route has only its own.
  • A label the alert doesn't have matches as the empty string. So env!="prod" and env="" both match an alert without env.
  • Regexes are fully anchored: service=~"api" matches api, not api-gateway. They follow Go RE2, as in Alertmanager: (?i) flags, ASCII-only \d, \w, \s, and POSIX classes such as [[:alpha:]].
  • Matchers are parsed the way Alertmanager parses them, quirks included. Verified against Alertmanager shows how this is tested against Alertmanager itself.

Options

Flag What it does --firing 'label=value,...' Another alert firing at the same time. Repeat for more alerts. Shows whether an inhibit rule mutes this alert (details) --format json JSON output. text is the default --input-format, --matcher-strategy As for check

--format json prints labels, receivers, and for every matched route its path, the effective settings, and set_by: the route that set each value. A value missing from set_by is Alertmanager's default. It also has firing, inhibited and inhibited_by (rule, line, column, and the source alert that matched).

Limits

  • A config Alertmanager would refuse to load exits 2 and names the route at fault: a regex RE2 rejects, a malformed duration, matchers on the root route. So does a label that isn't label=value.
  • A regex with Unicode classes such as \pL also exits 2, since amlint can't evaluate it the way Go does. Check those routes with amtool config routes test.

docs.title: Check whether an alert is muted
docs.text:
--firing adds another alert that fires at the same time, as comma-separated label=value pairs. Quote a value that contains a comma: summary="a, b". Repeat the flag for more alerts. amlint then checks the config's inhibit_rules and shows the rule that mutes (inhibits) the alert, if any:

amlint route alertmanager.yml alertname=DiskFull instance=db-1 team=infra \
  --firing 'alertname=NodeDown,instance=db-1'

  Labels  alertname=DiskFull, instance=db-1, team=infra
  Firing  alertname=NodeDown, instance=db-1

  route → route.routes[0]
    receiver          infra-slack          set here
    group_by          alertname, cluster   inherited from route
    group_wait        10s                  set here
    group_interval    5m                   Alertmanager default
    repeat_interval   4h                   Alertmanager default

────────────────────────────────────────
  Inhibited by inhibit_rules[1]  ·  alertmanager.yml:42:5
     while firing: alertname=NodeDown, instance=db-1
  Routed to: infra-slack, but no notification is sent while it is inhibited.

The alert is muted when, for some rule:

  • the alert matches the rule's target_matchers,
  • a firing alert matches its source_matchers, and
  • every label in equal has the same value on both alerts. A label missing on both counts as equal, since Alertmanager compares missing labels as "".

Good to know

  • An alert never mutes itself, and alerts that match both sides of a rule don't mute each other.
  • A firing alert still mutes others when it is muted or silenced itself, as in Alertmanager.
  • Rules are checked in order. The first one that applies is shown.
  • source_matchers / target_matchers and the older source_match / source_match_re / target_match / target_match_re both work, with the same anchored RE2 regexes as routes.
  • Muting doesn't change routing: the alert lands on the same routes, but Alertmanager sends no notification for it.
  • An inhibit rule amlint can't evaluate exits 2, but only when you pass --firing.

docs.title: Test your routing
docs.text:
test runs unit tests for your routing tree. For each set of alert labels, you state which receivers the alert must reach. It uses the same simulation as route, against the local file: no running Alertmanager or Go toolchain needed.

amlint test alertmanager.yml routing-tests.yml

routing-tests.yml is a list of cases:

- name: critical infra alerts page infra and the on-call
  labels: {team: infra, severity: critical}
  expect: [infra-pager, pager]

- name: warning infra alerts go to slack only
  labels: {team: infra, severity: warning}
  expect: [infra-slack]

- name: unrelated alerts aren't swallowed
  labels: {team: unknown}
  expect: [default]

  ✓  critical infra alerts page infra and the on-call
  ✓  warning infra alerts go to slack only
  ✓  unrelated alerts aren't swallowed
────────────────────────────────────────
  3 passed

Each case has labels:, an optional name:, and exactly one of these assertions:

Key Passes when the alert reaches expect: [a, b] exactly these receivers, in any order receiver: name exactly this one receiver receivers: [a, b] exactly these receivers, in this order (continue: true fan-out follows definition order) drop: true no receiver at all

The cases can also sit under a top-level tests: key.

A failing case shows what differs, and which routes the alert matched. Had the second case said expect: [infra-slack, pager]:

  ✓  critical infra alerts page infra and the on-call
  ✗  warning infra alerts go to slack only
     labels:    team=infra, severity=warning
     expected:  infra-slack, pager
     actual:    infra-slack
       - pager  expected, not delivered
     routes:    route.routes[0]

────────────────────────────────────────
  1 failed  ·  1 passed

test exits 1 if any case fails, and 2 if the config can't be simulated (see route) or the tests file isn't a list of cases.

Options

Flag What it does --coverage List the routes no case reaches, with file:line:col, and the coverage percentage (details) --fail-under N Exit 1 if route coverage is below N% (0 to 100). Turns on --coverage --format json JSON output. text is the default --input-format, --matcher-strategy As for check

--format json gives one object per case, with passed, expected, actual, missing, unexpected, the matched routes, and the inhibition fields (firing, expected_inhibited, inhibited, inhibited_by). A malformed case has error instead.

docs.title: Test inhibition
docs.text:
A case can list firing:, the labels of other alerts firing at the same time, and assert inhibited: true or inhibited: false. amlint checks it the same way as route --firing:

- name: disk alerts are muted while their node is down
  labels: {alertname: DiskFull, instance: db-1, team: db}
  firing:
    - {alertname: NodeDown, instance: db-1}
  expect: [db-slack]       # where it is routed
  inhibited: true          # ...and that nothing is sent

- name: another node's outage doesn't mute it
  labels: {alertname: DiskFull, instance: db-1, team: db}
  firing:
    - {alertname: NodeDown, instance: db-2}
  expect: [db-slack]       # firing: without inhibited: expects inhibited: false
  • inhibited: goes next to a receiver assertion, which still checks routing, or on its own.
  • With firing: and no inhibited:, the case expects the alert not to be muted.
  • A case that fails on inhibition names the rule. Had the second case listed NodeDown on db-1:
  ✗  another node's outage doesn't mute it
     labels:    alertname=DiskFull, instance=db-1, team=db
     firing:    alertname=NodeDown, instance=db-1
     expected:  db-slack
     actual:    db-slack
     inhibited: expected no, actual yes
       by inhibit_rules[1]  ·  alertmanager.yml:42:5  ·  while firing: alertname=NodeDown, instance=db-1
     routes:    route.routes[2]

docs.title: Measure route coverage
docs.text:
--coverage lists the routes no case reaches, so you can see what your tests miss:

amlint test alertmanager.yml routing-tests.yml --coverage

  ✓  critical infra alerts page infra and the on-call
  ✓  warning infra alerts go to slack only
  ✓  unrelated alerts aren't swallowed
────────────────────────────────────────
  3 passed

  Route coverage  4 of 6 routes  ·  66.7%
  Not matched by any test case:
    route.routes[2]             alertmanager.yml:18:7    {team="db"}  →  db-slack
    route.routes[2].routes[0]   alertmanager.yml:21:11   {severity="critical"}  →  db-pager
  • A route is covered when a case's alert passes through it: the route it lands on, that route's parents, and every branch of a continue: true fan-out. The root route counts too.
  • Failing cases count. Malformed ones don't, since they aren't routed.
  • Some routes can't be covered. Above, route.routes[2].routes[0] is unreachable: route.routes[1] takes every critical alert first. A case for {team: db, severity: critical} shows it going to pager.
  • --fail-under N exits 1 when coverage is below N%. The percentage is rounded to one decimal before the comparison, and is only 100 when every route is covered.

With --format json and coverage on, the output is an object instead of a list:

{
  "tests": [ ... ],
  "coverage": {
    "routes": 6, "covered": 4, "percent": 66.7, "fail_under": 90.0,
    "uncovered": [
      {"path": "route.routes[2]", "line": 18, "column": 7},
      {"path": "route.routes[2].routes[0]", "line": 21, "column": 11}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Review a config change
docs.text:
diff compares two versions of a config, old first. It shows the findings the change fixed or added, and the alerts it routes differently. Use it on pull requests to catch regressions.

amlint diff main.yml alertmanager.yml

  FIXED  [undefined-receiver]  ·  main.yml:6:7  ·  route.routes[1]
     Route references receiver 'db-pager' which is not defined in receivers. Alertmanager refuses to load this config.

  NEW    [empty-receiver]  ·  alertmanager.yml:15:5  ·  receivers[db-slack]
     Receiver 'db-slack' has no integration configured (no slack_configs, pagerduty_configs, webhook_configs, etc.). Alerts sent here will be silently dropped.

────────────────────────────────────────
  1 fixed  ·  1 new  ·  1 unchanged

──────────────── Routing ────────────────

  team=infra
    infra-slack  group_wait   30s → 10s
    and 1 more label set with the same change

  team=db, severity=critical
    receivers   db-pager → db-slack

  2 routing changes  · 6 label sets checked

diff exits 1 if the new config has any new finding, and 0 otherwise.

Options

Flag What it does --format FORMAT text (default), json, or markdown (PR comment) --no-routing Compare findings only; skip the routing comparison --ignore CODE Skip these checks. Comma-separate the codes or repeat the flag --only CODE Consider only these checks. Comma-separate the codes or repeat the flag --input-format, --matcher-strategy As for check

--format json gives the added and fixed findings (lines from the new file for added, the old one for fixed), the unchanged count, and a routing object: checked, truncated and changes (each with labels, differences, the full old / new routes and the number of similar label sets), or skipped with the reason.

Good to know

  • A finding counts as unchanged when its code and config path (such as route.routes[1]) are the same in both files. Moving a route can show its findings as fixed and new.
  • An empty old file (/dev/null, or a config that is new in a PR) counts as no config at all: every finding is new, none is fixed, and every label set's receivers were (none) before.

docs.title: Routing changes
docs.text:
After the findings, diff sends the same label sets (sample alerts) through both configs, with the same simulation as route, and lists the ones that come out differently.

  • A label set shows up when its receivers change, or when a receiver it reaches gets a different group_by, group_wait, group_interval, repeat_interval or time intervals.
  • Edits that still deliver every alert the same way don't show up: match: rewritten as matchers:, or reordered siblings that never match the same alert.
  • Label sets with exactly the same change are folded into one, shown with the smallest label set.
  • Routing changes don't affect the exit code, since a PR that edits routing usually means to.
  • If either config can't be simulated (see route), the section says why, and the findings diff still runs.
How amlint picks the label sets

The label sets come from the matchers of both configs: for every label, the values used with = and !=, a few strings each =~ / !~ regex fully matches, and the label being absent. Small configs get every combination. Larger ones get, for every route, a label set that reaches it and one that stops on it, then single-label variations of those, spread evenly over the routes and capped at 5000 label sets. The summary says when the cap was hit.

docs.title: Post the diff as a PR comment
docs.text:
--format markdown prints a compact report for a pull-request comment:

amlint diff main.yml alertmanager.yml --format markdown

### amlint diff

**2 routing changes** · **1 new finding** · 1 fixed · 1 unchanged · 6 label sets checked

#### Receivers

| labels | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `team=db, severity=critical` | `db-pager` | `db-slack` |

#### Grouping and timings

| labels | receiver | setting | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `team=infra` (+1 similar) | `infra-slack` | `group_wait` | `30s` | `10s` |

#### Changed routes

Green: added · yellow: changed · red, dashed: removed · grey: unchanged routes, folded.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    r["(root)<br/>→ default"]
    r_0["{team=#34;infra#34;}<br/>→ infra-slack<br/>group_wait: unset → 10s"]
    r --> r_0
    r_1["{team=#34;db#34;, severity=#34;critical#34;}<br/>→ db-slack<br/>receiver: db-pager → db-slack"]
    r --> r_1
    classDef changed fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700,color:#1f2328
    class r_0,r_1 changed
```

#### New findings

| level | check | location | message |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ⚠ warning | `empty-receiver` | `alertmanager.yml:15:5` (`receivers[db-slack]`) | Receiver 'db-slack' has no integration configured (no slack\_configs, pagerduty\_configs, webhook\_configs, etc.). Alerts sent here will be silently dropped. |

#### Fixed findings

| level | check | location | message |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ✖ error | `undefined-receiver` | `main.yml:6:7` (`route.routes[1]`) | Route references receiver 'db-pager' which is not defined in receivers. Alertmanager refuses to load this config. |
  • The summary line always comes first. Each table appears only when it has rows, so an unchanged config gives just the heading and the summary.
  • (+1 similar) means one more label set with exactly the same change.
  • Changed routes is a Mermaid diagram, which GitHub draws in the comment. It shows the routes that were added, removed or changed, with what changed, and the routes above them. Unchanged siblings fold into one grey node. Routes are matched by their matchers, so a route inserted at the top doesn't make every route below it look changed, but a new order of the same routes does: the first match wins. It stops after 40 routes.
  • New findings point into the new file, fixed ones into the old file.
  • Each table stops after 50 rows with …and N more, so a large config can't produce a huge comment.
  • The output is deterministic. Names from the config are escaped, so a receiver called @team doesn't ping anyone.
  • Exit codes are the same as for text output.

The GitHub Action posts this report as a PR comment and keeps it up to date.

docs.title: Run amlint in CI
docs.text: The GitHub Action does all of this for GitHub with a few inputs. To run the CLI yourself:

docs.title: Fail the build on findings
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/alertmanager.yml
name: Lint Alertmanager config

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: pip install amlint
      - run: amlint check alertmanager.yml --strict

--strict fails the build on WARN findings too. For a report that never fails the build, use --exit-zero instead.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Command 0 1 2 check No ERROR findings (WARN and INFO pass unless --strict) An ERROR finding, or a WARN with --strict Input can't be read (see below) diff No new findings A new finding Input can't be read test Every case passes and coverage meets --fail-under A case fails, or coverage is below --fail-under Input can't be read, the config can't be simulated, or the tests file isn't a list of cases route The alert was routed, delivered or not — Input can't be read, the config can't be simulated, or a label isn't label=value tree Always, findings or not — No root route, or input can't be read

"Input can't be read" means: file not found, YAML that doesn't parse, a file that isn't an Alertmanager config in the format given or detected, or, for check --rules, a glob that matches no files or a rule file that can't be read. --exit-zero turns 1 into 0, but not 2.

docs.title: Annotate the PR diff
docs.text:
--format github prints workflow commands that GitHub shows as annotations on the PR diff. You don't need SARIF or Code Scanning:

- name: Lint Alertmanager config
  run: amlint check alertmanager.yml --strict --format github

::error file=alertmanager.yml,line=6,col=7,title=amlint undefined-receiver::Route references receiver 'db-pager' which is not defined in receivers. Alertmanager refuses to load this config. (route.routes[1])
::notice file=alertmanager.yml,line=1,col=1,title=amlint global-resolve-timeout-missing::global.resolve_timeout is not set, so Alertmanager uses 5m. It only applies to alerts sent without an end time; Prometheus always sets one. (global)

ERROR becomes ::error, WARN ::warning and INFO ::notice. Paths are made relative to $GITHUB_WORKSPACE, so annotations land on the right file even when you pass an absolute path. Exit codes are the same as for text output.

docs.title: Upload to GitHub Code Scanning
docs.text:
SARIF output lets GitHub Code Scanning show findings on the PR diff, on the line each finding points at. The job needs the security-events: write permission:

- name: Run amlint
  run: amlint check alertmanager.yml --format sarif --exit-zero > results.sarif

- name: Upload to GitHub Code Scanning
  uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
  with:
    sarif_file: results.sarif

--exit-zero keeps the upload step running when amlint finds errors. Fail the build in a separate amlint check step.

docs.title: Catch regressions on a PR
docs.text:
- name: Check for regressions
  run: |
    git show origin/main:alertmanager.yml > /tmp/main.yml
    amlint diff /tmp/main.yml alertmanager.yml

To get the routing diff as a PR comment, use the GitHub Action's diff-base input.

docs.title: See findings in your editor
docs.text:
