amlint lsp is a language server. Your editor starts it and shows amlint's findings as you type, on the lines amlint check reports. You don't run it yourself.

  • Findings come from the editor buffer, so you don't have to save first. Each check code links to its docs.
  • Hover on a route shows its matchers, receiver, group_by and timings, where each value comes from, and an example alert that ends there. It is the same simulation as route.
  • Quick fixes add # amlint: disable=<code> to the line, or # amlint: disable-file=<code> to the top of the file.

It reads every format check reads. YAML files without an Alertmanager config, such as Kubernetes manifests, get no findings.

ignore and severity come from the project config in the workspace folder, or next to the file when it isn't in one. The --rules checks don't run in the editor.

Setup for VS Code, Neovim and Helix: Editors.

docs.title: List all checks
docs.text:
amlint list

Prints every check code with its level, a one-line description, and a ✓ in the amtool column when amtool check-config catches it too. Those are configs Alertmanager refuses to load. The rest load fine but don't behave as intended. Details for each check are in Checks.

docs.title: Explain one check
docs.text:
amlint explain undefined-receiver
amlint explain inhibit-no-equal

Shows the check's level, whether amtool catches it, why it matters, and a bad and a fixed example. Useful when a finding is unfamiliar, or for onboarding. An unknown code exits 2 and lists the valid ones.

docs.title: Start a new config
docs.text:
init prints a minimal valid alertmanager.yml to start from:

amlint init > alertmanager.yml

docs.title: Checks overview
docs.text:
amlint's checks catch Alertmanager config mistakes that lose alerts, send them to the wrong place, or mute them when they shouldn't be.

amlint has 38 checks. amtool check-config also catches 20 of them: Alertmanager refuses to load those configs, and amlint reports them so one run covers everything. The other 18 are configs that amtool accepts and Alertmanager runs, just not the way you meant. Those are the main reason to run amlint.

The three Prometheus rules checks run only with amlint check --rules, which compares your routes and inhibition rules with the alerts your Prometheus rule files define. See Prometheus rules.

From the CLI, amlint list prints the same list, and amlint explain <code> explains one check.

docs.title: All checks
docs.text:
Grouped by page, then by level. ✓ in the amtool column means amtool check-config catches it too.

area check level amtool what it flags Routing no-root-route error ✓ The config has no route: key. Routing invalid-root-route error ✓ The root route has no receiver, or has matchers, continue: true or time intervals. Routing undefined-receiver error ✓ A route names a receiver that isn't defined in receivers:. Routing groupby-ellipsis error ✓ group_by lists '...' next to label names. Routing bad-regex error ✓ A regex doesn't compile, or uses syntax Go RE2 doesn't support, like lookahead. Routing bad-matcher error ✓ A matchers: entry Alertmanager can't parse. Routing bad-match-label error ✓ A match: or match_re: key that isn't a classic label name, like k8s.ns. Routing unreachable-route warn A catch-all route without continue: true hides the sibling routes after it. Routing route-match-collision warn Two sibling routes have identical matchers; the second never gets alerts. Routing shadowed-route warn An earlier sibling route matches every alert this route matches; this one never gets alerts. Routing stripped-brace warn A bare matcher value ends in }, which Alertmanager strips off. Routing useless-continue info continue: true on the last sibling route does nothing. Routing deep-nesting info The routing tree is more than 5 levels deep. Receivers duplicate-receiver error ✓ Two receivers share the same name. Receivers email-no-smarthost error ✓ An email_configs entry has no smarthost, and global.smtp_smarthost isn't set. Receivers webhook-no-url error ✓ A webhook_configs entry has no url or url_file. Receivers pagerduty-no-routing-key error ✓ A pagerduty_configs entry has no routing_key or service_key (or their _file forms). Receivers slack-no-api-url error ✓ A slack_configs entry has no api_url, and global.slack_api_url isn't set. Receivers opsgenie-no-api-key error ✓ An opsgenie_configs entry has no api_key, and global.opsgenie_api_key isn't set. Receivers msteams-no-webhook-url error ✓ An msteams_configs entry has no webhook_url or webhook_url_file. Receivers telegram-no-bot-token error ✓ A telegram_configs entry has no bot_token or bot_token_file. Receivers discord-no-webhook-url error ✓ A discord_configs entry has no webhook_url or webhook_url_file. Receivers victorops-no-api-key error ✓ A victorops_configs entry has no api_key, and global.victorops_api_key isn't set. Receivers wechat-no-corp-id error ✓ A wechat_configs entry has no corp_id, and global.wechat_api_corp_id isn't set. Receivers sns-no-target error ✓ An sns_configs entry has none of topic_arn, phone_number or target_arn. Receivers template-file-missing error A relative templates: path matches no file next to the config (warn for a glob). Receivers empty-receiver warn A receiver has no integration, like slack_configs (info for the root route's receiver or one named like null). Receivers unused-receiver info A receiver no route uses. Inhibition inhibit-no-equal warn An inhibition rule has no equal: field. Inhibition circular-inhibition warn Two inhibition rules can mute each other. Inhibition inhibit-same-match info The source and target side of an inhibition rule share a label="value". Timing undefined-time-interval error ✓ mute_time_intervals or active_time_intervals names an interval that isn't defined. Timing repeat-before-group warn repeat_interval is shorter than group_interval. Timing wait-exceeds-interval warn group_wait is longer than group_interval. Timing global-resolve-timeout-missing info global.resolve_timeout isn't set, so Alertmanager uses its default of 5m. Prometheus rules route-unknown-alertname warn With --rules: a route matches an alertname no alerting rule produces. Prometheus rules inhibit-unknown-alertname warn With --rules: an inhibition rule's source or target matches an alertname no alerting rule produces. Prometheus rules alert-hits-default-receiver info With --rules: alerts match no child route, by their static labels, and go to the root route's receiver.

docs.title: Severity levels
docs.text:
level meaning error Alertmanager refuses the config, or notifications can't be delivered as configured. warn The config loads, but almost certainly doesn't do what you meant. info Worth a look. Often intentional.

amlint check exits 1 on an error finding. Warnings fail it only with --strict. See exit codes.

docs.title: Ignoring checks
docs.text:
For a whole repo: list checks to skip, or change a check's level, in .amlint.yml in the directory you run amlint from ([tool.amlint] in pyproject.toml works too). See project config.

.amlint.yml
ignore:
  - unused-receiver
severity:
  empty-receiver: info       # warn → info
  deep-nesting: warn         # info → warn

For one run: amlint check alertmanager.yml --ignore deep-nesting,unused-receiver, or --only bad-regex to show nothing else.

For one spot in the config: add a comment, so the exception and its reason sit next to the config. See inline suppressions.

# amlint: disable-file=global-resolve-timeout-missing

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: catch-all   # amlint: disable=unreachable-route
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: infra
  • # amlint: disable=<code>,<code> at the end of a line silences those checks on that line.
  • The same comment on a line of its own silences them on the next line of YAML.
  • # amlint: disable-file=<code>,<code> in the comment block at the top of the file, before any YAML, silences them for the whole file.

A finding's line is the one amlint prints with it.

docs.title: Inhibition checks
docs.text:
These checks catch inhibition rules that mute more alerts than you meant, or that mute each other so nobody gets notified.

An inhibition rule (an entry under inhibit_rules:) mutes alerts that match its target matchers while an alert that matches its source matchers is firing, but only when both alerts have the same values for the labels listed in equal:. Matchers are label conditions such as severity="critical". amlint reads both styles: source_matchers / target_matchers, and the older source_match / source_match_re / target_match / target_match_re.

To see whether one alert mutes another, run amlint route alertmanager.yml alertname=DiskFull --firing 'alertname=NodeDown'.

docs.title: inhibit-no-equal
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: An inhibition rule has no equal: field, so source and target alerts don't need to have anything in common.

Bad
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    # no equal:

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. While any critical alert fires, it mutes every warning alert, in every cluster and service. A critical alert in one service hides warnings from unrelated ones.

How to fix: List the labels that tie a target alert to its source, such as the alert name and the cluster.

Fixed
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    equal: [alertname, cluster]   # only mute warnings of the same alert on the same cluster

Limits: Rules with no source matchers at all are not flagged. Every alert counts as their source, so they mute their targets whenever any alert that isn't a target fires. That is a deliberate "always mute" pattern: kube-prometheus uses it to keep its InfoInhibitor alert quiet.

docs.title: circular-inhibition
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: Two inhibition rules can mute each other: the source of each rule matches the target of the other.

Bad
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    equal: [alertname]
  - source_matchers: [severity="warning"]    # the first rule's target...
    target_matchers: [severity="critical"]   # ...mutes the first rule's source
    equal: [alertname]

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. When a critical and a warning alert with the same alertname fire together, each mutes the other, and you get no notification for either. A muted alert still mutes others.

How to fix: Keep only the direction you need, usually the more severe alert muting the less severe one.

Fixed
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning"]
    equal: [alertname]

Limits: amlint compares only the label="value" matchers of each side. Regex and != matchers are ignored, so a pair of rules that differ only in those can still be flagged.

docs.title: inhibit-same-match
docs.text:
Level: info · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: The source and target side of an inhibition rule require the same label="value", such as severity="critical" on both sides. The rule then mutes alerts of the same kind as the alerts that trigger it.

Bad
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical", env="prod"]
    target_matchers: [severity="critical", team="infra"]   # same severity as the source
    equal: [alertname]

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. A critical env="prod" alert mutes critical team="infra" alerts with the same alertname, including ones that are sources of this rule themselves. An alert never mutes itself, and two alerts that both match both sides don't mute each other. If both sides match exactly the same alerts, the rule mutes nothing.

How to fix: If a critical alert should only mute less severe ones, change the target side. If critical alerts are meant to mute other critical alerts, keep the rule and turn the finding off with # amlint: disable=inhibit-same-match at the end of the rule's first line.

Fixed
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="critical", env="prod"]
    target_matchers: [severity="warning", team="infra"]
    equal: [alertname]

Limits: Like circular-inhibition, this compares only label="value" matchers.

docs.title: Receiver checks
docs.text:
A receiver is a named destination for alerts: routes (the branches of the route: tree that pick alerts by their labels) send each alert to one. Each receiver holds one or more integrations, such as slack_configs, pagerduty_configs, email_configs or webhook_configs, which do the actual sending. These checks catch receivers that can't deliver (a duplicate name, no integration, a missing URL, key or template file) and receivers that no route uses.

amtool below is amtool check-config, Alertmanager's own config checker. "Also catches it" means Alertmanager refuses the config anyway. "Doesn't catch it" means Alertmanager loads and runs the config without complaint, so only amlint tells you.

docs.title: duplicate-receiver
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: Two receivers have the same name.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/team'
  - name: team                  # same name again
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/oncall'

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config (notification config name "team" is not unique). It doesn't use one and ignore the other. amlint points at the second definition.

How to fix: Rename one of them, or merge them, because one receiver can hold several integrations.

RenameMerge 
receivers:
  - name: team
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/team'
  - name: team-oncall         # point the route that needs it here
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/oncall'

receivers:
  - name: team
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/team'
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/oncall'

docs.title: empty-receiver
docs.text:
Level: warn, or info when the drop looks intentional · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: A receiver has no integration, so alerts routed to it go nowhere. An empty list such as webhook_configs: [] also counts as no integration.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/default'
  - name: pager                 # no integration

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config and routes critical alerts to pager. Then it silently drops them.

How to fix: Add an integration. If you mean to drop the alerts, make that clear: make it the default receiver (the receiver: at the top of route:), or name it null, blackhole, devnull, dev-null, discard or drop (in any case). amlint then reports it as info, not warn.

FixedIntentional drop 
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/default'
  - name: pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: 'your-pagerduty-integration-key'

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [alertname="Watchdog"]
      receiver: 'null'
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/default'
  - name: 'null'              # drops Watchdog on purpose: info, not warn

Quote 'null'. Unquoted, YAML reads null as no value, not as the name null.

Limits: amlint knows these integrations: email, pagerduty, slack, opsgenie, victorops, webhook, wechat, sns, msteams, msteamsv2, telegram, discord, pushover, webex, jira, rocketchat, incidentio and mattermost (each as <name>_configs). It reports a receiver that uses only some other key as empty.

docs.title: unused-receiver
docs.text:
Level: info · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: A receiver is defined, but no route sends alerts to it. Usually it's left over from an older config.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/default'
  - name: old-pager             # no route uses it
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: 'your-pagerduty-integration-key'

What Alertmanager does: Loads it and never sends anything to it. That's harmless, but it's clutter, and readers may think alerts go there.

How to fix: Delete the receiver, or add a route that uses it.

Delete itRoute to it 
route:
  receiver: default
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/default'

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: old-pager
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://hooks.example.com/default'
  - name: old-pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: 'your-pagerduty-integration-key'

docs.title: template-file-missing
docs.text:
Level: error for a file path, warn for a glob · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: A relative path under templates: matches no file. These files hold the notification templates ({{ define "..." }}) that your integrations use.

Bad
templates:
  - templates/custom.tmpl       # no such file next to alertmanager.yml: error
  - tmpl/*.tmpl                 # glob that matches no file: warn

What Alertmanager does: Resolves relative paths against the config file's directory. It starts even when a path matches nothing, but it loads no templates from that path, so notifications that use those templates fail to render.

How to fix: Correct the path, or add the file. Paths are relative to the config file.

Fixed
templates:
  - templates/custom.tmpl       # exists next to alertmanager.yml
  - templates/*.tmpl            # matches at least one file

Limits:

  • amlint doesn't check absolute paths (/etc/alertmanager/templates/*.tmpl). They point into the Alertmanager host or container, not to where amlint runs.
  • amlint doesn't run this check on a plain config read from stdin (amlint check -), because there's no directory to resolve the paths against.
  • For a Kubernetes Secret or kube-prometheus-stack values, amlint checks entries against the template files that ship with the config, not against files on disk. See Kubernetes & Mimir.

docs.title: Missing integration fields
docs.text:
Each integration needs one field before it can send anything: a server, a URL, a key or a target. If that field is missing, Alertmanager rejects the whole config. It won't start, and a reload fails and keeps the old config. All of these checks are error level, and amtool also catches them. amlint includes them so that one run reports every problem, as text, JSON or SARIF, without the Go binary.

check integration needs or instead email-no-smarthost email_configs smarthost global.smtp_smarthost webhook-no-url webhook_configs url url_file pagerduty-no-routing-key pagerduty_configs routing_key routing_key_file, service_key, service_key_file slack-no-api-url slack_configs api_url api_url_file, global.slack_api_url, global.slack_api_url_file opsgenie-no-api-key opsgenie_configs api_key api_key_file, global.opsgenie_api_key, global.opsgenie_api_key_file msteams-no-webhook-url msteams_configs webhook_url webhook_url_file telegram-no-bot-token telegram_configs bot_token bot_token_file discord-no-webhook-url discord_configs webhook_url webhook_url_file victorops-no-api-key victorops_configs api_key api_key_file, global.victorops_api_key, global.victorops_api_key_file wechat-no-corp-id wechat_configs corp_id global.wechat_api_corp_id sns-no-target sns_configs one of topic_arn, phone_number, target_arn none
  • A *_file field reads the value from a file, which keeps the secret out of the config.
  • A global.* field is the default for every entry of that integration that doesn't set its own.
  • A field set to an empty string (url: '') counts as missing.

docs.title: email-no-smarthost
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: An email_configs entry has no smarthost (the SMTP server, as host:port), and global.smtp_smarthost isn't set.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    email_configs:
      - to: 'team@example.com'
        from: 'alertmanager@example.com'
        # no smarthost

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set smarthost on the entry, or set global.smtp_smarthost once for all email entries.

On the entryGlobal default 
receivers:
  - name: team
    email_configs:
      - to: 'team@example.com'
        from: 'alertmanager@example.com'
        smarthost: 'smtp.example.com:587'

global:
  smtp_smarthost: 'smtp.example.com:587'
  smtp_from: 'alertmanager@example.com'
receivers:
  - name: team
    email_configs:
      - to: 'team@example.com'

docs.title: webhook-no-url
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A webhook_configs entry has no url and no url_file.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    webhook_configs:
      - send_resolved: true     # no url

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set url, or set url_file to read the URL from a file.

Fixed
receivers:
  - name: team
    webhook_configs:
      - url: 'http://my-service/webhook'
        send_resolved: true

docs.title: pagerduty-no-routing-key
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A pagerduty_configs entry has no PagerDuty integration key. None of routing_key, routing_key_file, service_key or service_key_file is set.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - severity: critical      # no routing_key

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set routing_key, or routing_key_file to read it from a file. amlint also accepts service_key and service_key_file.

Fixed
receivers:
  - name: pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: 'your-pagerduty-integration-key'
        severity: critical

docs.title: slack-no-api-url
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A slack_configs entry has no Slack webhook URL. It has no api_url or api_url_file, and neither global.slack_api_url nor global.slack_api_url_file is set. amlint also flags an empty api_url: '', even when a global URL is set.

Bad: no URLBad: empty api_url 
receivers:
  - name: team
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts'    # no api_url, and no global one

global:
  slack_api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXXX'
receivers:
  - name: team
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts'
        api_url: ''           # empty: the global URL isn't used

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config. An empty api_url doesn't fall back to the global URL. Alertmanager tries to read the empty string as a URL, and that fails.

How to fix: Set api_url (or api_url_file) on the entry, or set global.slack_api_url (or global.slack_api_url_file) once for all Slack entries. Delete any empty api_url: line.

On the entryGlobal default 
receivers:
  - name: team
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXXX'
        channel: '#alerts'

global:
  slack_api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXXX'
receivers:
  - name: team
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts'

docs.title: opsgenie-no-api-key
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: An opsgenie_configs entry has no api_key or api_key_file, and neither global.opsgenie_api_key nor global.opsgenie_api_key_file is set.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    opsgenie_configs:
      - priority: P1            # no api_key

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set api_key (or api_key_file) on the entry, or set global.opsgenie_api_key (or global.opsgenie_api_key_file) once for all OpsGenie entries.

On the entryGlobal default 
receivers:
  - name: team
    opsgenie_configs:
      - api_key: 'your-opsgenie-api-key'
        priority: P1

global:
  opsgenie_api_key: 'your-opsgenie-api-key'
receivers:
  - name: team
    opsgenie_configs:
      - priority: P1

docs.title: msteams-no-webhook-url
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: An msteams_configs entry has no webhook_url and no webhook_url_file.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    msteams_configs:
      - title: 'Alert'          # no webhook_url

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set webhook_url to the Teams incoming webhook URL, or set webhook_url_file to read it from a file.

Fixed
receivers:
  - name: team
    msteams_configs:
      - webhook_url: 'https://outlook.office.com/webhook/...'
        title: 'Alert'

docs.title: telegram-no-bot-token
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A telegram_configs entry has no bot_token and no bot_token_file.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    telegram_configs:
      - chat_id: -1001234567890   # no bot_token

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set bot_token, or set bot_token_file to read it from a file.

Fixed
receivers:
  - name: team
    telegram_configs:
      - bot_token: '123456:ABC-DEF...'
        chat_id: -1001234567890

docs.title: discord-no-webhook-url
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A discord_configs entry has no webhook_url and no webhook_url_file.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    discord_configs:
      - title: 'Alert'          # no webhook_url

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set webhook_url to the channel's webhook URL, or set webhook_url_file to read it from a file.

Fixed
receivers:
  - name: team
    discord_configs:
      - webhook_url: 'https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...'
        title: 'Alert'

docs.title: victorops-no-api-key
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A victorops_configs entry has no api_key or api_key_file, and neither global.victorops_api_key nor global.victorops_api_key_file is set.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    victorops_configs:
      - routing_key: 'team-routing-key'   # no api_key

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set api_key (or api_key_file) on the entry, or set global.victorops_api_key (or global.victorops_api_key_file) once for all VictorOps entries.

On the entryGlobal default 
receivers:
  - name: team
    victorops_configs:
      - api_key: 'your-victorops-api-key'
        routing_key: 'team-routing-key'

global:
  victorops_api_key: 'your-victorops-api-key'
receivers:
  - name: team
    victorops_configs:
      - routing_key: 'team-routing-key'

docs.title: wechat-no-corp-id
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A wechat_configs entry has no corp_id (your WeChat Work enterprise ID), and global.wechat_api_corp_id isn't set. There's no *_file variant for this field.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    wechat_configs:
      - agent_id: '1000002'     # no corp_id
        api_secret: 'your-api-secret'

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set corp_id on the entry, or set global.wechat_api_corp_id once for all WeChat entries.

On the entryGlobal default 
receivers:
  - name: team
    wechat_configs:
      - corp_id: 'your-corp-id'
        agent_id: '1000002'
        api_secret: 'your-api-secret'

global:
  wechat_api_corp_id: 'your-corp-id'
receivers:
  - name: team
    wechat_configs:
      - agent_id: '1000002'
        api_secret: 'your-api-secret'

docs.title: sns-no-target
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: An sns_configs entry has no destination. None of topic_arn, phone_number or target_arn is set.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: team
    sns_configs:
      - sigv4:
          region: us-east-2
        # no topic_arn, phone_number or target_arn

What Alertmanager does: Rejects the config.

How to fix: Set one of topic_arn (an SNS topic), phone_number (SMS) or target_arn (a mobile push endpoint).

Fixed
receivers:
  - name: team
    sns_configs:
      - topic_arn: 'arn:aws:sns:us-east-2:123456789012:My-Topic'
        sigv4:
          region: us-east-2

docs.title: Routing checks
docs.text:
These checks catch two kinds of routing mistakes: a routing tree Alertmanager refuses to load, and routes that load fine but never get the alerts you meant for them.

A route is a node in the route: tree. Its matchers (label conditions such as severity="critical", written under matchers:, match: or match_re:) pick alerts, and its receiver (a named entry under receivers:) gets them. Routes in the same routes: list are siblings: Alertmanager tries them top to bottom and stops at the first match, unless that route sets continue: true ("keep trying the siblings below me").

To see where a given alert ends up, run amlint route alertmanager.yml team=infra severity=critical.

docs.title: no-root-route
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: The config has no route: key, so there is no routing tree.

Bad
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://alerts.example.com/hook

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config: no routes provided.

How to fix: Add a root route that names the receiver every alert falls back to.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://alerts.example.com/hook

docs.title: invalid-root-route
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: The root route (the top-level route:, which every alert enters) breaks one of Alertmanager's rules for it. It must name a receiver, and it can't have matchers, continue: true, mute_time_intervals or active_time_intervals.

Bad
route:
  matchers: [team="infra"]   # the root route must match every alert
  routes:                    # ...and it has no receiver
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config, with an error such as root route must specify a default receiver or root route must not have any matchers. amlint reports every broken rule at once.

How to fix: Give the root route a receiver. Move matchers and time intervals down to a child route.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default          # gets every alert no child route matches
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager

docs.title: undefined-receiver
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A route names a receiver that isn't defined under receivers:.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: pager-team   # not defined below
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://alerts.example.com/hook

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config: undefined receiver "pager-team" used in route.

How to fix: Define the receiver, or correct the name to one that exists.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: pager-team
receivers:
  - name: default
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://alerts.example.com/hook
  - name: pager-team         # added
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: <integration-key>

docs.title: groupby-ellipsis
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A route's group_by (the labels that decide which alerts share one notification) lists '...' next to label names. '...' already means "group by every label".

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  group_by: ['...', alertname, cluster]

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config: cannot have wildcard group_by (`...`) and other labels at the same time.

How to fix: Keep either '...' or the label names, not both.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  group_by: [alertname, cluster]   # or: ['...']

docs.title: bad-regex
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A regex matcher (=~ or !~) doesn't compile, or uses syntax that Go's RE2 engine, which Alertmanager uses, doesn't have: lookahead or lookbehind, backreferences, possessive quantifiers, atomic groups, or a repeat count over 1000. amlint checks regexes in routes and in inhibition rules.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - service=~"(?!test-).*"   # lookahead: RE2 has none
      receiver: team

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the whole config (error parsing regexp: invalid or unsupported Perl syntax), so no route works, not just this one.

How to fix: Rewrite the regex in RE2 syntax. To exclude values, use a negative matcher (!~) instead of a lookahead.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - service!~"test-.*"       # every service not starting with test-
      receiver: team

docs.title: bad-matcher
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: An entry under matchers: (or source_matchers: / target_matchers: in an inhibition rule) is not a matcher Alertmanager can parse. Common causes:

  • an empty matcher between two commas: a=b,,c=d
  • a stray double quote: a=b"c
  • a comma in a bare (unquoted) value, which splits the entry: a=b, c=~x{1,2}
  • a quoted label name, such as "service.name"=..., followed by a value that isn't a valid Go string: "x.y"="a\.b" (\. is not a Go escape), or a bare value with a backslash or brace ("x.y"=~\d+)
Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - 'service=api,,env=prod'        # empty matcher between the commas
        - '"service.name"=~"api\.v2"'   # \. is not a Go escape
      receiver: team

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config (bad matcher format: ... or matcher value contains unescaped double quote: ...). It reads each entry with its classic parser, and with its UTF-8 parser only if the classic one fails. amlint flags the entries both parsers reject.

How to fix: Write each matcher as label="value" (or !=, =~, !~), with one comma between matchers. A quoted label name sends the whole entry to the UTF-8 parser, where values are Go strings: quote the value and double each backslash.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - 'service="api", env="prod"'
        - '"service.name"=~"api\\.v2"'  # \\ is one backslash in a Go string
      receiver: team

docs.title: bad-match-label
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A key under match: or match_re: isn't a classic label name: a letter or underscore, then letters, digits and underscores ([a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*). Inhibition rules' source_match, target_match and their _re forms are checked too. Names like k8s.namespace only work in matchers:, quoted.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - match:
        k8s.namespace: payments   # not a classic label name
      receiver: payments

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config: invalid label name "k8s.namespace".

How to fix: Move the matcher to matchers: (or source_matchers: / target_matchers:) and quote the label name. For a child route or an inhibition rule, the amlint finding spells out the entry to use.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - '"k8s.namespace"="payments"'   # quoted: any UTF-8 name works
      receiver: payments

docs.title: unreachable-route
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: A catch-all route (no matchers, or only label=~".*" matchers) without continue: true sits above other siblings. It takes every alert, so the siblings below it never get any.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: team-slack       # no matchers: matches every alert
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager            # never reached

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. Every alert goes to team-slack and stops there, so pager never gets an alert.

How to fix: Put the catch-all last. If every alert should reach the catch-all and the routes below it, give it continue: true.

Catch-all lastNotify both Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
    - receiver: team-slack
Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: team-slack
      continue: true         # keep trying the routes below
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager

docs.title: route-match-collision
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: Two sibling routes have identical matchers, and the first one has no continue: true. Different spellings of the same matcher count as identical: match: {team: infra} and matchers: [team="infra"].

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="critical"]   # same matchers
      receiver: infra-slack                            # never reached

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. Every matching alert stops at the first route, so infra-slack never gets an alert.

How to fix: If both receivers should get these alerts, add continue: true to the first route. Otherwise, give the second route different matchers, or remove it.

Notify bothDifferent matchers Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
      continue: true         # keep trying the routes below
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="critical"]
      receiver: infra-slack
Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
    - matchers: [team="infra", severity="warning"]
      receiver: infra-slack

docs.title: shadowed-route
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: An earlier sibling without continue: true matches every alert this route matches, even though their matchers differ. amlint compares the label values each matcher allows, not how it's written. In each pair below, the earlier route hides the later one:

  • severity=~"warning|critical" before severity="critical": critical matches the regex
  • team!="db" before team="infra": infra is not db
  • alertname=~"Kube.*" before alertname=~"KubePod.*": every KubePod… name starts with Kube
  • service!~"db-.*" before service=~"api-[0-9]+": no api-… name starts with db-
  • team=~"|infra" before team="": a missing label counts as the empty string, as in Alertmanager
  • severity="critical" before severity="critical", team="infra": the earlier route asks for less

Parent routes count too, because every alert that reaches the siblings matched their parents. Under a parent with env="prod", a sibling with env=~"prod|staging", severity="critical" hides a later sibling with severity="critical".

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity=~"warning|critical"]
      receiver: ops
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]   # never reached
      receiver: pager

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. Critical alerts match the first route and stop there, so pager never gets them.

How to fix: Put the narrower route first. If both receivers should get the alerts, give the broader route continue: true instead.

Narrower firstNotify both Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager
    - matchers: [severity=~"warning|critical"]
      receiver: ops
Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity=~"warning|critical"]
      receiver: ops
      continue: true         # keep trying the routes below
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager

Limits: amlint reports only routes it can prove dead. It stays silent when a regex uses case folding ((?i)), word boundaries (\b), anchors anywhere but the very start or end, or is too large to compare, even if the route is in fact dead. Each dead route gets one finding: identical matchers are route-match-collision, and a catch-all sibling is unreachable-route.

docs.title: stripped-brace
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: A bare (unquoted) value at the end of a matchers: entry ends in }, and the entry doesn't start with {. Alertmanager drops that }. Entries in routes and in inhibition rules' source_matchers / target_matchers are checked.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - code=~[0-9]{3}      # Alertmanager reads the regex as [0-9]{3
      receiver: http-errors

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. Its classic matcher parser strips one trailing } from every entry, braces or not. The regex here becomes [0-9]{3, which matches the text 1{3 and not 123, so the route never matches the alerts you meant.

How to fix: Quote the value, or wrap the whole entry in braces.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - code=~"[0-9]{3}"    # or: '{code=~[0-9]{3}}'
      receiver: http-errors

docs.title: useless-continue
docs.text:
Level: info · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: The last route in a routes: list has continue: true. No sibling comes after it, so the flag does nothing.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [env="prod"]
      receiver: team
      continue: true           # last sibling: nothing to continue to

What Alertmanager does: Ignores the flag. continue only passes the alert on to later siblings in the same routes: list, never to the routes after the parent.

How to fix: Remove continue: true. If you meant alerts to also reach the routes after the parent, set continue: true on the parent instead.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [env="prod"]
      receiver: team

docs.title: deep-nesting
docs.text:
Level: info · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: The routing tree goes more than 5 levels below the root route. That is hard to read, review and debug.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [env="prod"]
      routes:
        - matchers: [region="eu"]
          routes:
            - matchers: [team="infra"]
              routes:
                - matchers: [service="db"]
                  routes:
                    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
                      routes:
                        - matchers: [component="disk"]   # level 6
                          receiver: db-pager

What Alertmanager does: Routes alerts as usual. It has no depth limit.

How to fix: Flatten the tree. One route with several matchers replaces a chain of single-matcher routes.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - env="prod"
        - region="eu"
        - team="infra"
        - service="db"
        - severity="critical"
        - component="disk"
      receiver: db-pager

docs.title: Prometheus rules checks
docs.text:
These checks compare your Alertmanager config with your Prometheus alerting rules, the alert: rules in Prometheus rule files that fire alerts named after the rule. They catch parts of alertmanager.yml that wait for an alert no rule fires (usually a typo or a renamed rule), and alerts that fall through to your catch-all destination because nothing more specific picks them up. They run only when you pass your rule files with --rules:

amlint check alertmanager.yml --rules 'rules/*.yml'

docs.title: Which rule files amlint reads
docs.text:
• Quote the glob so that amlint expands it, not your shell. ** matches subdirectories: --rules 'rules/**/*.yml'.
  • Repeat --rules for more locations: --rules 'rules/*.yml' --rules 'k8s/prometheusrules/*.yaml'.
  • amlint reads Prometheus rule files (groups[].rules[]), the format that Prometheus, Thanos, Mimir and the Loki ruler use. It also reads prometheus-operator PrometheusRule manifests (spec.groups): several in one file separated by ---, or a kind: List as kubectl get prometheusrules -o yaml prints it.
  • Only alerting rules (alert:) count. amlint skips recording rules (record:).
  • If a glob matches no file, or a file can't be parsed, amlint exits with code 2. If the files contain no alerting rules, amlint prints a warning and skips these checks.

docs.title: What amlint knows about an alert
docs.text:
Alertmanager routes an alert by its labels: each route, a branch of the route: tree, sends the alerts its matchers select to a receiver, a named notification destination. At runtime an alert gets its labels from four places:

  1. the series that the rule's PromQL expr returns (instance, job, namespace, ...)
  2. the rule's labels:
  3. alertname, which is always the rule's name
  4. Prometheus' external_labels, the labels a Prometheus server adds to every alert it sends (set in prometheus.yml, often cluster or region)

Only 2 and 3 are in the rule file. Together they are the rule's static labels, and amlint checks routing with those. This matters because routes often match on labels that only exist at runtime, such as namespace or cluster, and amlint can only be sure about the labels it can see. So:

  • A label whose value is a Go template (team: '{{ $labels.owner }}') has an unknown value.
  • A label that routes match on but that no rule sets (namespace, cluster, job) is assumed to come from the series or external_labels, so its value is unknown too.
  • A label that some rules set but this rule doesn't is treated as absent, the way Alertmanager would see it. That's how amlint catches a rule that forgot its severity label.

When a result depends on a label with an unknown value, amlint reports nothing rather than guess. amlint also can't see alert_relabel_configs in Prometheus, which can change labels on the way out.

All three checks are warn or info, never error. amtool check-config, Alertmanager's own config checker, catches none of them, because the config itself is valid. Each finding points at a line in alertmanager.yml, so # amlint: disable=<code> comments work there as usual.

docs.title: route-unknown-alertname
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: A route matches an alertname that no alerting rule in your --rules files fires. Usually the name has a typo, or the rule was renamed or removed.

rules/node.yml
groups:
  - name: node
    rules:
      - alert: HighCPUUsage
        expr: node_cpu_busy > 0.9
alertmanager.yml (bad)
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [alertname="HighCpuUsage"]   # no rule fires this name
      receiver: infra-pager

  ⚠  WARN   [route-unknown-alertname]  ·  alertmanager.yml:4:7  ·  route.routes[0]
     Route matches alertname 'HighCpuUsage', which no alerting rule in the --rules files
     produces — did you mean 'HighCPUUsage'? Unless such alerts come from another source,
     this branch is dead.

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config and runs. The route never receives the alert it was written for, so the alert goes to whichever route matches it instead, often the default receiver.

How to fix: Use the exact rule name. The finding suggests the closest one.

alertmanager.yml (fixed)
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [alertname="HighCPUUsage"]
      receiver: infra-pager

What amlint checks in matchers:, match: and match_re::

  • alertname="X" (or match: {alertname: X}): X must be a rule's name.
  • A regex that just lists names, such as alertname=~"A|B|C" (or ^(?:A|B|C)$): amlint checks each name on its own, so it reports one misspelled entry in a long list.
  • Any other regex, such as alertname=~"Kube.*": amlint reports it when it matches none of the alert names. Like Alertmanager, it anchors the regex at both ends and uses Go RE2 syntax.
  • != and !~: excluding a name that nothing fires excludes nothing, so that's probably a typo too.

Limits: Alerts that don't come from these rule files (another Prometheus, Loki, Grafana, a script posting to the Alertmanager API) also look unknown. Pass their rule files too, or add # amlint: disable=route-unknown-alertname to that route.

docs.title: inhibit-unknown-alertname
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: An inhibit rule (a rule that mutes alerts matching its target while an alert matching its source is firing) has a source or target that matches an alertname no alerting rule fires. amlint checks source_match, source_match_re and source_matchers, and the same target_* keys, with the same matching as route-unknown-alertname.

rules/node.yml
groups:
  - name: node
    rules:
      - alert: NodeDown
        expr: up{job="node"} == 0
      - alert: NodeHighLoad
        expr: node_load5 > 10
alertmanager.yml (bad)
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [alertname="NodeDwn"]   # typo: no rule fires this
    target_matchers: [alertname="NodeHighLoad"]
    equal: [instance]

What Alertmanager does: Loads the rule and gives no sign of a problem. If the source never fires, the rule never mutes anything. If the target never fires, the rule has nothing to mute.

How to fix: Use the exact rule names.

alertmanager.yml (fixed)
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [alertname="NodeDown"]
    target_matchers: [alertname="NodeHighLoad"]
    equal: [instance]

Limits: The same as for route-unknown-alertname. Alerts from other sources look unknown.

docs.title: alert-hits-default-receiver
docs.text:
Level: info · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: Based on its static labels, an alert matches none of the child routes (the routes: under the top-level route:), so it goes to the default receiver, the receiver: set at the top of route:. Typically the rule forgot its severity or team label, or uses a value that no route handles.

rules/app.yml
groups:
  - name: app
    rules:
      - alert: DiskFull
        expr: disk_free_ratio < 0.05
        labels:
          severity: critical
      - alert: QueueBacklog
        expr: queue_depth > 1000   # no severity label
alertmanager.yml
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="critical"]
      receiver: pager

  ℹ  INFO   [alert-hits-default-receiver]  ·  alertmanager.yml:1:1  ·  route
     Based on static rule labels, 1 alert with no severity label matches no child route and
     goes to the root receiver 'default': QueueBacklog (rules/app.yml:8). Labels from the
     PromQL series or external_labels may still route it elsewhere at runtime.

What Alertmanager does: Delivers these alerts to the default receiver, which is often a channel nobody watches.

How to fix: Add the missing label to the rule, or add a route for the alert.

rules/app.yml (fixed)
groups:
  - name: app
    rules:
      - alert: DiskFull
        expr: disk_free_ratio < 0.05
        labels:
          severity: critical
      - alert: QueueBacklog
        expr: queue_depth > 1000
        labels:
          severity: critical

If some alerts should use the default receiver, give them a route of their own (alertname=~"A|B" to default). That also documents the choice. Or turn the check off for the file with # amlint: disable-file=alert-hits-default-receiver.

How findings are grouped: amlint routes each rule with the same simulation as amlint route. You get one finding per combination of the label values that the routes match on, and each finding names the first five alerts. So if you send every warning to the default receiver on purpose, as kube-prometheus does, you get one finding for severity=warning, however many warning alerts there are. A rule that lacks a label the other rules set gets a finding of its own ("with no severity label"). All of these findings point at the root route:.

Limits:

  • It's info, not warn, because static labels aren't the whole story. amlint treats a label that this rule doesn't set as absent. If the label actually comes from the PromQL series or external_labels, the alert may still route elsewhere at runtime.
  • amlint skips an alert when its route depends on a label with an unknown value (see above).
  • If the root route has no child routes, everything goes to its receiver by design, and the check stays quiet.

docs.title: Timing checks
docs.text:
These checks catch notification timing that doesn't do what it says, and routes that point at time intervals that don't exist.

Alertmanager batches alerts into groups (alerts on the same route that share its group_by labels) and times each group's notifications with three settings:

  • group_wait: how long to wait after a group's first alert before the first notification. Default 30s.
  • group_interval: how often to notify about changes, such as new or resolved alerts, to a group that was already notified. Default 5m.
  • repeat_interval: how long to wait before sending a notification again for alerts that are still firing and unchanged. Default 4h.

A child route inherits any of these it doesn't set from its parent, and the root route falls back to the defaults. amlint works out the values the same way, and reports a finding on the route that sets one of the two values involved.

docs.title: repeat-before-group
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: repeat_interval is shorter than group_interval.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  group_interval: 1h
  repeat_interval: 15m   # shorter than group_interval

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. After the first notification, Alertmanager sends a group's notifications only once per group_interval, and re-sends still-firing alerts at the first of those sends after repeat_interval has passed. So the reminders come every hour, not every 15 minutes.

How to fix: Make repeat_interval at least as long as group_interval, ideally a multiple of it. To get reminders more often, shorten group_interval too.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 15m   # a multiple of group_interval

docs.title: wait-exceeds-interval
docs.text:
Level: warn · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: group_wait is longer than group_interval. The two values are usually swapped: group_wait is meant to be a short pause that collects the first burst of alerts.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  group_wait: 10m       # wait 10 minutes before the first notification
  group_interval: 2m    # but report changes every 2 minutes

What Alertmanager does: Loads the config. A new group waits the full 10 minutes before its first notification; after that, changes go out every 2 minutes. The first notification about a new problem is the slowest one.

How to fix: Keep group_wait shorter than group_interval.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m

docs.title: undefined-time-interval
docs.text:
Level: error · amtool: also catches it

What goes wrong: A route's mute_time_intervals (mute the route during these times) or active_time_intervals (send only during these times) names an interval that isn't defined under time_intervals:.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: infra
      mute_time_intervals: [maintenance]   # not defined anywhere

What Alertmanager does: Refuses to load the config: undefined time interval "maintenance" used in route.

How to fix: Define the interval under time_intervals:, or fix the name. Intervals defined under the older top-level mute_time_intervals: key count too.

Fixed
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="infra"]
      receiver: infra
      mute_time_intervals: [maintenance]
time_intervals:
  - name: maintenance
    time_intervals:
      - weekdays: [saturday, sunday]

docs.title: global-resolve-timeout-missing
docs.text:
Level: info · amtool: doesn't catch it

What goes wrong: global.resolve_timeout isn't set, so Alertmanager uses its default of 5m. Nothing breaks; the value just isn't visible in your config.

Bad
route:
  receiver: default
# no global.resolve_timeout

What Alertmanager does: Uses resolve_timeout only for alerts that arrive without an end time (endsAt): if such an alert isn't sent again within that time, Alertmanager marks it resolved. Prometheus always sets an end time, so this setting doesn't change alerts that come from Prometheus.

How to fix: Set the value you want. If all your alerts come from Prometheus, you can ignore this check instead (see Ignoring checks).

Fixed
global:
  resolve_timeout: 5m
route:
  receiver: default

docs.title: Playground
docs.text:
Paste your alertmanager.yml, or the Kubernetes Secret, Helm values, Mimir config or AlertmanagerConfig resources that hold it, and amlint checks it as you type. You see the findings and the lines they point at, the route tree, where an alert is delivered, and how a change affects routing. Add Prometheus alerting rules to check routes against the alerts that exist.

Your config stays in your browser. amlint runs in this page as Python compiled to WebAssembly. Nothing you paste or type is uploaded, and once the page has loaded it needs no network.

How it works, and limits
  • The page downloads Pyodide (Python for the browser) from the jsDelivr CDN, plus the amlint wheel built from this site's sources. Your browser caches them, so later visits start faster. None of the page's requests contains your config.
  • Checks run in a Web Worker (a background thread of the page) and call amlint's own --format json output, so the results match amlint check, amlint route and amlint diff.
  • Share link puts the config, compressed, into the URL after #. Browsers don't send that part to any server, including this one. But anyone you give the link to can read the config, so remove secrets first; the page lists the lines that may hold them.
  • The page doesn't keep your config anywhere. Reload it and your edits are gone.
  • template-file-missing isn't checked for a plain alertmanager.yml, because its template files aren't in the browser. Run amlint check on your machine or in CI for that. Template files that ship in a Secret or in Helm values are checked under Findings, but not in the Diff tab.
